events.title: Wormholes and the Imaginary Distance Bound
events.abstract: Some of the simplest wormhole solutions involve massless scalar fields that take imaginary values. Massless fields can be interpreted as coupling constants in asymptotically flat or asymptotically AdS gravity theories. We argue that wormhole effects imply an imaginary distance bound, an upper limit for the analytic continuation of the theory to imaginary values of these couplings. In string theory examples, we find explicit effects that render the low-energy theory invalid either before or precisely at this wormhole limit. We argue that the existence of such effects enforcing the distance bound is a general feature of string theories containing wormholes. In some cases, the bounds we discuss coincide with the weak gravity conjecture, and with the Kontsevich-Segal-Witten condition on complex metrics.

events.title: Accelerating Dark Matter Searches Using Grover's Algorithm
events.abstract: I will show that Grover's algorithm can be used to parametrically accelerate wave-like dark matter searches. Despite having a finite coherence time, wavelike dark matter can imprint a coherent, O(1) phase onto a sensor through a dispersive coupling over an integration time which significantly exceeds its coherence time. This phase can be transferred to a qubit register and then digitized, after which the qubits are available for quantum computational processing in which dark matter acts as a coherent gate. If the sensor is prepared in a superposition of frequencies, Grover's algorithm can then be used to speed up a search for dark matter in N frequency bins by a factor of sqrt(N). Although the technological challenges to implementing such a search remain substantial, this demonstrates that there is no fundamental obstruction to accelerating wave-like dark matter searches with quantum computational techniques over many coherence times.

events.title: A Landscape of Candidate de Sitter Vacua in String Theory
events.abstract: String theory provides our most developed framework for unifying quantum mechanics and gravity. To connect it to the physics of our Universe, we need to understand how ten-dimensional geometry gives rise to four-dimensional cosmology. In this talk, I will discuss recent progress in this quest, drawing on new analytic techniques and large-scale computations. I will explain how quantised fluxes give rise to a landscape of vacua and how we search it for solutions with specific physical properties. I will highlight our recent construction of explicit candidate de Sitter vacua and discuss new mechanisms for generating such solutions. I will also briefly describe how AI can guide these searches and help develop new algorithms for studying string compactifications.

events.title: A Few Thoughts on Flavor and CP violation
events.abstract: I will present recent works motivated by suggestive patterns observed in high-precision measurements of flavor and CP violating observables. First, I will discuss CKM unitarity constraints, focusing on the unitarity triangle angles and the remarkable hints of spontaneous CP violation. Then, I will highlight that Standard Model Yukawa running suggests quark–lepton unification at an interesting low scale, of about 10^6 GeV, with the Pati–Salam model as a compelling candidate.

events.title: Can one hear the shape of a black hole singularity?
events.abstract: The approach to a black hole singularity is described by an interior cosmological spacetime. I will explain how key geometric features of this interior spacetime are audible in the asymptotic, large overtone quasinormal modes of the black hole. In a holographic setting the quasinormal modes are the basic excitations of the dual, nonzero temperature, quantum field theory.

events.title: Galactic Axion Factories: Astrophysical Axions and the Many Ways to Catch Them
events.abstract: Axions and axion-like particles (ALPs) can have weak couplings to the Standard Model which may be magnified in extreme astrophysical environments, opening unique pathways toward observational signatures. In this talk, I will discuss several exciting ways such signatures can manifest. I will begin with an overview of astrophysical light-shining-through-wall setups and novel searches for axion production at the galactic stellar population level. This will then segue to ongoing theoretical and experimental efforts to build GALAXIS, an all-sky MeV gamma-ray satellite mission designed to search for axions from core-collapse supernovae. I will then discuss a further extension to compact objects, highlighting recent work searching for axions via black hole superradiance and gravitational wave signatures. Throughout, I highlight how these diverse astrophysical environments, together with a new generation of upcoming observations, can open new windows on axion parameter space with real potential for discovery.

PRESENT and FUTURE of the European X-ray free electron laser
events.abstract: Abstract: X-ray Free Electron Lasers (XFELs) have greatly enhanced our ability to observe the dynamics of nuclei and electrons in real time at atomic resolution, thereby deepening our fundamental understanding of matter across different disciplines. They have also started to produce first results in other scientific areas, for instance, nuclear physics. Following a brief summary of the current landscape of XFELs with key parameters, recent scientific breakthroughs, and landmark experiments, I will summarize some lessons learned with the first generation of XFEL operation. Then I will aim at answering the following questions: What comes after today's XFELs? How much better can XFELs become? Can we build fundamentally different XFELs? Will future XFELs be based on incremental improvements to existing facilities, or on fundamentally different accelerator concepts? How will experiments change? How can AI transform XFELs from user-operated instruments into increasingly autonomous scientific discovery platforms?

events.title: Single-Crystal Halide Perovskite Heterostructures
events.abstract:
Abstract: Layered heterostructures, formed one monolayer at a time, have been shown to host exotic emergent properties at the interfaces where two monolayers meet. Although impressive advances have been made in controlling these exquisite architectures, these approaches do not readily lead to scalable and reproducible syntheses of well-defined interfaces. This motivates the synthesis of bulk crystalline solids, where the solution-state chemistry, and not the fabrication method, forms the heterostructure. We recently reported a synthetic strategy for the self-assembly of layered perovskite–non-perovskite heterostructures as single crystals in solution, where organic molecules directed the assembly [1]. I will present various layered heterostructures that form as an interleaving of perovskite slabs with a different inorganic slab and describe the unusual optoelectronic [2,3] and magnetic [4] phenomena that arise in these materials. I will also discuss the reactivity of coordination complexes placed within these nonporous solids.
[1] “Directed assembly of layered perovskite heterostructures as single crystals” Aubrey, Saldivar Valdes, Filip, Connor, Lindquist, Neaton, Karunadasa, Nature, 2021, 597, 355.
[2] “Tuning the quantum-well structure of single-crystal layered perovskite heterostructures” Deshmukh, Chen, Cleron, Tie, Wen, Heinz, Filip, Karunadasa, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2025, 147, 40171.
[3] “Twisted tin-chloride perovskite single-crystal heterostructures” Cleron, Chen, Pan, Saha, Marlton, Stolz, Li, Dionne, Liu, Filip, Karunadasa, Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 2025, e20140.
[4] “Isolation of diamond spin chains in a layered halide perovskite heterostructure” Caniglia, Li, Wen, Brueggemeyer, Lee, Solomon, Fisher, Karunadasa, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2025, 147, 28340.

events.title: How to Spot a Supernova from Deep Underground
events.abstract: Abstract: Stellar core collapses create enormous bursts of tens-of-MeV neutrinos on a timescale of a few tens of seconds after collapse and preceding optical fireworks by hours or days. These neutrinos can be observed in underground neutrino detectors worldwide. The neutrinos themselves carry directional information that can be exploited to determine the position of the supernova (or of the compact remnant, in the case of failed explosion) on the sky. I will give an overview of methods for low-latency pointing to core-collapse events with neutrino detectors.

Progress toward a sterile neutrino search with optically levitated nanospheres
events.abstract: The origin and nature of neutrino masses remain key open questions in particle physics. With a simple extension to the Standard Model, light neutrino masses can arise via the seesaw mechanism, in which each mass state has a heavy right-handed counterpart. In some models, these right-handed “sterile” states fall in the keV to MeV mass range. The Quantum Invisible Particle Sensor (QuIPS) collaboration is developing a search for sterile neutrinos utilizing silica nanospheres trapped at the focus of a laser in high vacuum. Due to their extreme isolation from the environment, such levitated optomechanical systems have opened up new pathways for testing fundamental physics with quantum-limited sensitivity. If the nanospheres are doped with beta or electron capture isotopes, detection of the recoil impulse accompanying the emission of decay products enables an event-by-event measurement of the total momentum carried away, including by otherwise invisible particles. The Yale QuIPS team has already demonstrated impulse sensitivity of better than 50 keV/c, sufficient to resolve collisions of individual gas atoms with a nanosphere and well below the momentum carried by neutrinos in typical decays. In this talk I will present an overview of the experiment, showcase recent progress, and discuss prospects for a first sterile neutrino search.

Diffraction from first principles
events.abstract: Diffractive processes comprise nearly half the cross section at the LHC, and are a key probe of phenomena ranging from Regge (forward) physics, to the behavior of cosmic ray showers, to the saturation of nuclear matter. Diffractive processes exhibit unique properties like forward scattering and large “rapidity gaps” of the detector devoid of particles that have so far defied a systematic field theory description. We use effective field theory techniques to describe diffraction from first principles, opening up new frontiers for exploration at the dawn of the EIC, HL-LHC, and FAIR accelerators.

events.title: Axion Interactions with Topological Defects
events.abstract: In this talk, we explore how the compact field space of axions shapes their interactions with topological defects. We first show how virtual monopole loops generate an axion potential through the Witten effect, including discussing the theories with fermions, and give an example in which this potential dominates the axion mass. We then turn to superconducting axion strings, discussing the impact of an explicit PQ breaking mass term on the superconducting zero modes which live on the string.

The Magnus expansion and its classical limit
events.abstract: The Magnus expansion has recently emerged as an alternative to the conventional Dyson expansion in QFT. In the Magnus expansion, we perturbatively expand the logarithm of the S-matrix. The matrix elements of this logarithm are Magnus amplitudes, which have many pleasing properties, including a well-behaved classical limit. In this talk we will introduce the Magnus expansion and explain its diagrammatic formulation. Then, we will study the classical limit of certain Magnus amplitudes and show explicitly that they are free of classically singular terms. Our analysis will rely on an algebra of permutations, which we will also use to derive new closed-form expressions for Murua coefficients at any loop order. Based on: 2512.05017 and 2609.40291.

events.title: The Dark Dimension, Revisited
events.abstract: Motivated by the swampland program, it has been proposed that a tower of massive Kaluza-Klein (KK) gravitons from a compactified flat extra dimension can be dark matter, with the heavier modes constantly cascading to lighter ones. The phenomenology crucially depends on the rate at which a massive KK mode decays to lighter modes. We show that, up to mild assumptions on the UV theory, the decay rate is suppressed by a factor of (q/m)^4 compared to the one commonly used in the literature, where q is the momentum of the decay products and m is the mass of the decaying KK mode. This suggests that the proposed scenario is ruled out by CMB observations by many orders of magnitude. Remarkably, the same suppression opens up a vastly different parameter space in which KK gravitons from a strongly warped extra dimension (e.g. a Randall-Sundrum setup) are a viable dark matter candidate, either as the cascading gravitons themselves or as a stable component of the tower.

events.title: Learning the Geometry of the Physical World: From Shape Understanding to Scientific Discovery
events.host_org: AI + Data for Science (CS 292, EE 292R, PSYCH 292R, STATS 282)
events.abstract: Much of science is fundamentally geometric. Scientific observations arise on irregular domains, and scientific discoveries often depend on comparing structures, identifying correspondences, and understanding how quantities vary or transform. In this talk we first discuss the PointNet and PointNet++ architectures that helped free deep learning from the tyranny of regular grids, introducing models capable of learning directly from unordered geometric data. This made deep learning applicable to a much broader class of structures, including those that arise naturally in science—from molecules and particle collisions to the distribution of galaxies. We transition to presenting our Vector Neurons work aimed at designing neural architectures with built in invariances and equivariances important in physics. Finally we show how our work on functional maps transformed correspondence from a problem of matching individual points into a problem of transporting functions and information between geometric domains. This provides a powerful mathematical foundation for comparing scientific structures, transferring measurements, and identifying meaningful patterns of variation. Together, these ideas suggest a path toward AI systems that understand not just individual scientific observations, but the structural relationships connecting them.

events.title: Detecting coordinated behavior across multiple fully encrypted domains
events.host_org: AI + Data for Science (CS 292, EE 292R, PSYCH 292R, STATS 282)
events.abstract: Coordinated inauthentic behavior threatens societal stability, markets, and security. Advances in generative AI amplify these threats, enabling effortless content creation, amplifying actors’ influence. Detection is hindered by cross-domain activity, where pseudonymous profiles operate across encrypted platforms, and by privacy constraints limiting content analysis. We develop a robust and scalable cross-domain identity matching framework, based on bursty dynamics, independent of content or interaction data. It outperforms state-of-the-art temporal and structural approaches, remains resilient to incomplete data, and is fairly stable over time. By framing identity matching within the “network of networks” perspective, we demonstrate how coordinated behavior propagates across domains. This dual methodological and theoretical contribution paves the way for innovative strategies to combat digital threats in an increasingly complex, encrypted, and adversarial landscape. Joint work with Shahar Somin, Jeremy Kepner, and Tom Cohen.

AI methods that effectively leverage multi-modal data hold transformative potential for biomedical discovery and clinical care. events.title: Decrypting the Brain with AI
events.host_org: AI + Data for Science (CS 292, EE 292R, PSYCH 292R, STATS 282)
events.abstract: You … your memories and ambitions, your sense of personal identity and free will, are in fact no more than the behavior of a vast assembly of nerve cells …” Crick’s words capture the profound challenge of decrypting the neural code. This challenge has long been hindered by two limitations: our ability to record activity from large neuronal populations under the complex, variable conditions in which brains evolved, and our capacity to model the intricate relationships between stimuli, behaviors, and neural activity. Recent breakthroughs are beginning to overcome these barriers. Cutting-edge technologies now enable large-scale recordings, while AI can construct predictive brain models that link stimuli, neural activity, and behavior. These digital twins open the door to virtually limitless in silico experiments, testing theories that would otherwise be impossible to probe at scale in living brains. I will discuss our work building brain foundation models and digital twins to uncover the mechanisms of neural representation, with predictions validated through closed-loop experiments.

events.title: A Resource Rational Analysis of Representations: Geometry, Inference, Capacity
events.location: Stanford Neurosciences Building, James Lin and Nisa Leung Seminar Room, E153
events.abstract:
Abstract
Neural systems process information by forming representations of the world. Studies of representational geometry have revealed remarkably structured representations in biological and artificial systems, as well as surprising alignment in representations across systems. Why do representations across systems converge to similar structures, how do these structures encode concepts and uncertainty over them, and how are they shaped by resource constraints?
Here, we tackle these questions in neural networks through the lens of resource rationality, asking what representations are optimal for solving a task, given dimensionality and linear readout constraints. We derive a notion of optimal linear representations, and show that these emerge across varied architectures and tasks, providing a simple explanation for representational convergence as alignment toward the optimal solution. This shared treatment motivates a normative formalization of conceptual spaces that generalizes the linear representation hypothesis. We then extend this account to uncertainty and inference over conceptual spaces, asking how representations should change in response to in-context evidence, and finally to resource-constrained settings involving representational interference.
About the Center for Neural Data Science Seminar Series
The Center for Neural Data Science Seminar Series is a platform for trainees across campus to share insights and innovative approaches that bridge the gap between neuroscience and data science.
As neuroscience continues to generate vast amounts of data—from intricate neural circuit maps to large-scale brain activity recordings—the need for interdisciplinary expertise in data science, statistics, and engineering has never been more critical.
The Center for Neural Data Science mission is to advance brain research through the development of cutting-edge analytical methodologies and collaborative approaches. Stanford's affiliates are invited to join this vibrant community dedicated to transformative discoveries.

Clinical Mind AI: Building an International AI Platform for Health Professions Education and the Learning Sciences
HAI Seminar with Marcos Santiago Rojas Pino and Thomas Caruso
Visit our website to learn more about the event agenda, speakers, and other details
Clinical Mind AI is a Stanford-developed, international collaborative platform designed to strengthen clinical reasoning education through AI-simulated patient encounters across health professions. The platform enables educators to create clinical cases aligned with their local curricula, learning goals, languages, and assessment needs, while giving learners repeated opportunities to practice open-ended history-taking, diagnostic reasoning, and communication. The seminar will present the motivation for Clinical Mind AI, its design principles, and how the platform is being used by educators and institutions across countries to support scalable, instructor-centered clinical simulation.
The talk will also discuss Clinical Mind AI as a research infrastructure for studying learning in clinical reasoning tasks. We will describe how learner interactions with AI-simulated patients can generate interpretable evidence about reasoning processes, including how students gather information, update hypotheses, document findings, and respond to feedback. The seminar will focus on broader questions at the intersection of AI, medical education, and learning science: how to build AI systems that preserve instructor agency, support multilingual and cross-institutional implementation, produce actionable insights for educators, and contribute to a more rigorous evidence base for AI-supported health professions education.

Abstract
The brain is a nonlinear dynamical system whose evolving population activity gives rise to computations that guide behavior. We will present a data-driven systems neuroscience framework that integrates large-scale neurophysiology, interpretable dynamical systems modeling, and targeted perturbations in cognitive animal models. This approach has enabled the discovery of cell-type-specific and brain-wide dynamical structures underlying reward and memory computations, including attractor manifolds that integrate past rewards and steer future decision-making. To enable causal tests and model-guided control of these computations, we have developed optical and genetic technologies for cellular-resolution, bidirectional control of neural populations, along with optimal control approaches for designing perturbations. Together, these converging advances set the stage for a closed-loop strategy to measure, model, and control neural dynamics and computations, toward the long-term vision of writing complex information into the brain.
Bio
YoungJu Jo is an Assistant Professor and the Brody Family Faculty Fellow in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute at the University of California, Berkeley. His laboratory develops and applies next-generation neurotechnologies to measure, model, and control neural dynamics and computations in behaving animals. He completed his postdoctoral training in Bioengineering in 2026, Ph.D. in Applied Physics in 2024, and M.S. in Biology in 2020, all at Stanford University, where he studied experimental and computational systems neuroscience with Profs. Karl Deisseroth, David Sussillo, and Krishna Shenoy. Before transitioning to neuroscience, he received his B.S. in Physics and Mathematics from KAIST in 2018, where he worked on computational imaging and optogenetics with Profs. YongKeun Park and Won Do Heo. His early work on AI-powered holographic microscopy was recognized with the 2022 Agarwal Award and commercialized by Tomocube.

Inference Auctions
events.abstract: When inference demand exceeds available compute capacity, model providers must decide which requests should be served first. Users have different tolerances for delay from an LLM API, but current priority pricing schemes compress these differences into coarse fixed-price service tiers. We design an inference auction that allows users to bid for faster service. Our auction allocates priority in an economically efficient way without sacrificing latency, and we develop fast algorithms for implementing prices that incentivize truthful bidding. We also design an autobidding agent for our inference auction, where users specify an inference budget and the autobidder dynamically adjusts its bids over time to maximize user utility subject to the budget constraint. Experiments validate the practicality of our auction: it increases system welfare while maintaining the cache utilization and latency advantages of SGLang, a state-of-the-art inference serving framework.

A Resolution of Friedgut's Conjecture on Influential Coalitions
events.abstract:
In Friedgut'04, the following conjecture was proposed: For any monotone Boolean function on [0,1]^n, there exists a coalition of o(n) coordinates and a target output b in {0, 1} such that after the remaining coordinates are sampled uniformly and independently, the coalition can choose its values to make the output of f equal to b with probability at least 0.99. We resolve this conjecture, showing that for any f, there exists such a coalition of size O(n / sqrt(log n)), biasing it towards some output.
In collective coin flipping, our result gives the first sublinear bound on the number of bad players that can bias any one-round coin flipping protocol with independent uniform messages, regardless of the message length. In pseudorandomness, this shows that deterministically extracting from NOSF sources with O(n / sqrt(log n)) bad coordinates is impossible.
A key ingredient in our proof is an encoding that lets us relate the influence of a function on a product space to the p-biased influence of the encoded function. We then rely on a structure theorem of Hatami'12 for functions with small p-biased influence to bias the encoded function.
Based on joint work with Eshan Chattopadhyay.

events.title: Low-error extractors
events.abstract:
We give the first explicit construction of low-error two-source extractors for min-entropy k = o(n). Our construction is based on a new regularity lemma for low-rank matrices, which provides the first polynomial bounds for the approximate duality conjecture. The key ingredient is a new result on rapid mixing in F2n, which shows that every spread set enjoys iterative sum-product type growth, under addition alone. Along the way, we explicitly construct new low-error affine extractors, and more.
Joint work with Dean Doron.

events.title: Reaching the Algorithmic Threshold for Tensor PCA via Local Markov Chains
events.abstract:
We study the tensor principal component analysis (tensor PCA problem) in the spiked tensor model, where the task is to recover an unknown vector on the signed hypercube {±1}N or the sphere 𝕊N−1(√N) from a noisy observation of its k-th tensor power, for some fixed k ≥ 3. This is a canonical planted problem in average case complexity, which exhibits a well-studied information-computation gap: global algorithms such as spectral methods and sum-of-squares work above an algorithmic threshold, below which we know matching lower bounds (against these and some other restricted models of computation).
In contrast, local algorithms such as Markov chains were only known to succeed from a random initialization at a polynomially larger signal-to-noise ratio, and were believed to be inferior to global algorithms for tensor PCA.
We show that two canonical local Markov chains, Glauber dynamics on the hypercube and Langevin dynamics on the sphere, once supplemented with annealing and ergodic averaging, achieve polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization. Our results demonstrate that algorithms based on local Markov chains can succeed all the way down to the algorithmic threshold for planted average-case problems, even from an uninformative cold start.
Based on joint works with Tselil Schramm.

events.title: Stanford Energy Seminar | More Value per Tonne: Rethinking How We Use Rock | Tiziana Vanorio, Stanford University
events.abstract:
Rocks may seem ordinary and ubiquitous, but they are the foundation of the geomaterials that underpin modern society—from cement in our built environment to the critical minerals in our smartphones and energy technologies. As the energy transition accelerates and demand for physical infrastructure grows, demand for materials is increasing rapidly. Simply extracting more resources to meet this demand is costly and environmentally consequential. Decades of innovation have made cars more fuel-efficient and batteries more effective; can we apply the same principle to Earth materials? Just as fuel efficiency asks how far we can go on a gallon of fuel, resource efficiency asks how much value we can obtain from a tonne of rock. Rocks themselves may be inexpensive, but extracting, processing, transporting, and developing or expanding the resource are not. Improving material retention and quarry utilization efficiency can therefore create more value from the resources we already extract.
This seminar explores three ways to make each tonne of rock more productive: retaining more usable material through feedstock redesign, extracting multiple values through water–rock interactions, and selecting better through smart sensing. Specifically, we will examine how feedstock redesign for cement can enable lower-temperature processing and decarbonization while conserving mass, increasing material yield and retention; how water interacting with rock under thermal and chemical gradients can mobilize valuable elements and create additional value streams; and how smart sensing could support more targeted extraction by revealing where valuable properties occur within heterogeneous rock resources. Ultimately, resource efficiency asks us to shift the question from how much we can extract to how much useful value we can obtain from what we extract.
Tiziana Vanorio, is a Professor of Geophysics in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford University, with a courtesy appointment in Civil and Environmental Engineering. She leads the Rock Physics and Geomaterials Laboratory, where her research investigates the physics of Earth materials and how their properties evolve through fluid interactions and mechanical and chemical transformations across scales. Her group integrates laboratory experiments, rock physics, and multiscale characterization to connect mineral and microstructural processes to the behavior of rocks and geomaterials. This understanding is used to engineer the subsurface and develop resource-efficient materials, including applications in geothermal systems, CO₂ mineralization, critical minerals, and new cementitious materials inspired by natural mineral transformation and cementation.

events.abstract:
The electrification of thermochemical processes with clean electricity has great potential as both an immediate and long-term solution towards the scalable decarbonization of chemical production. In this talk, I will discuss new paradigms in electrified thermochemical reactors based on high frequency electromagnetic fields. I will first discuss metamaterial reactors in which a volumetric open-cell lattice baffle is inductively heated with heating profiles tailored by reaction engineering considerations. I will next discuss resonant metamaterial reactors, a new class of reactor in which energy transduction is achieved by principles in resonant wireless power transfer. I will finally discuss how high frequency electric fields can be coupled to feedstocks and catalysts to facilitate new modes of selective energy transfer.

When Machines Read Politics: Agentic AI, Political Experts,and Measuring Energy Transition Policymaking Windows across 25 Countries
What explains cross-national variation in the political economy of the energy transition? Systematic comparisons of transition politics requires at scale measurements of hard-to-observe political factors, including policy support by legislators, political parties, national elites, courts, firms, financial regulators and the media, and how those commitments shift over time. In this talk, I will share results from a research programme that uses scaled agentic AI systems to collect, process and classify millions of parliamentary speeches, party manifestos, court decisions, media reports and regulatory records across 25 countries. The project also leverages in-depth qualitative human expert assessments of national-level political economy forces, capturing power relations absent from textual records. A Bayesian measurement model combines these diverse qualitative and quantitative empirical datastreams into per-country estimates of when and where energy policymaking windows are opening or closing. I will also reflect on when AI assessments of political power appear most accurate, and how AI and expert assessments of political economy can be combined to scale our understanding of the clean energy transition.
Bio:
Matto Mildenberger is Associate Professor of Political Science at the University of California Santa Barbara, where he also directs UCSB's 2035 Initiative, a campus-wide think-and-do tank developing applied, climate and energy policy roadmaps. Matto's research focuses on the political obstacles to climate and energy policy action and how both elites and publics make sense of climate policy.

events.title: The Future of Health in Africa: How U.S. Presidential Decisions Are Shaping a Generation of African Children - Dr. Ruth Gibson
events.abstract:
Session Description
The second Trump administration has undertaken a series of decisions with profound and lasting consequences for the health and survival of Africa’s children. The abrupt dismantling of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) is projected to result in approximately 14 million excess deaths, the majority concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa. Concurrently, the decision to initiate hostilities with Iran and the ensuing disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz have severely constrained global fertilizer exports to African markets. Modeling informed by NASA agricultural forecasts indicates that the 2027 growing season in the Sahel is at high risk of significant production shortfalls and elevated famine risk. This talk presents ongoing research from the Stanford Geopolitical Human Impact Research Lab on the cascading effects of geopolitical decisions on human health. It focuses specifically on the projected impacts of the Strait of Hormuz crisis on food security and child nutrition across the Sahel in the 2027 season and outlines concrete policy options through which the United States can still act to avert a larger-scale humanitarian catastrophe.
Speaker Bio
Dr. Ruth Gibson is the Founding Executive Director of the Stanford Geopolitical Human Impact Research Lab, the first research lab at Stanford University dedicated to examining how geopolitical decisions shape human lives, with particular attention to children. Based in the Department of Pediatrics at the School of Medicine, the Research Lab brings together health modeling, open-source intelligence, and international humanitarian law to produce rigorous, policy-relevant scholarship. She co-leads The Lancet Series on Foreign Engagement and Health in an Era of Geopolitical Crisis with Professor Gary Darmstadt. Dr. Gibson earned her PhD in geopolitical coercion and global health from the University of British Columbia and completed postdoctoral training at Stanford’s Center for International Security and Cooperation from 2022 to 2025. Drawing on more than a decade of international global health experience across five continents, her research focuses on the health consequences of sanctions, blockades, and armed conflict, especially their effects on maternal and child health.

events.title: Hospice 101
events.abstract:
Hospice has been part of the medical system in the US since the mid-1970s, yet there is still so much misinformation and misunderstanding about hospice and its role in providing the best possible care at the end of life.
Join us for this free webinar to debunk the myths about hospice and have your questions answered. You will learn what hospice is, why you might want hospice care for yourself or a loved one, when to start thinking about moving to hospice, and how to request it if you no longer want aggressive treatments and tests in the hospital. You will also learn how to cover the costs of hospice care, which is often covered at no cost through your Medicare contributions.
There will be time allowed for questions and resources will be provided, so you will leave the session better informed on this compassionate choice for end-of-life care.
This class will be recorded and a one-week link to the recording will be shared with all registered participants.

events.title: Cross-National Comparison of Long-Term Care Fraud Oversight and Investigation Practices in the United States, Japan, and South Korea
events.abstract:
As long-term care (LTC) services and public coverage expand, concerns about improper billing and fraudulent claims have also grown. These practices can divert public resources and place vulnerable beneficiaries at risk across LTC systems. In response, countries have developed approaches to identifying suspicious activities, investigating potential fraud, recovering improper payments, and imposing administrative, civil, or criminal consequences, reflecting the structure of their LTC systems and the types of misconduct they encounter. Although these systems differ across countries, cross-national comparison can reveal reciprocal policy and practice lessons regarding case triage, evidence development, interorganizational coordination, payment recovery, and enforcement. This study compares LTC fraud oversight and investigation practices in the United States, Japan, and South Korea to identify transferable lessons for developing effective and sustainable fraud-control systems that preserve continuity of care for residents.
Speaker: Hyunkyung "Yulia" Yun, PhD, MS, MSW, is an Assistant Professor at the Herbert Wertheim School of Public Health and Human Longevity Science, UC San Diego. She earned her PhD in Health Services Research, specializing in health economics, at the Brown University School of Public Health. Her research evaluates health policies and care delivery systems affecting older adults, focusing on long-term care, managed care, and quality of care, using causal inference methods with claims, assessment, and EMR data. Previously, she worked at South Korea's National Health Insurance Service as a fraud investigator and researcher supporting the country's long-term care insurance system.

events.title: Jonathan Kipnis - Navigating turbulent CNS waters
events.abstract:
Join the speaker for coffee, cookies, and conversation before the talk, starting at 11:45am.
Navigating turbulent CNS waters
Abstract
The central nervous system was long viewed as an immune-privileged organ, largely isolated from peripheral physiology. Over the past decade, this paradigm has shifted. Our work has revealed that the brain continuously exchanges signals, cells, and molecules with the immune and lymphatic systems, and that these interactions are essential for normal brain function, aging, and disease. In this lecture, I will discuss recent discoveries that redefine the anatomical and physiological pathways connecting the brain to the rest of the body, including meningeal lymphatics, skull and vertebral bone marrow, and cerebrospinal fluid dynamics. I will also present emerging evidence that dysfunction of these systems contributes to neurological disorders and cognitive decline, highlighting new therapeutic opportunities at the interface of neuroscience and immunology.
Jonathan Kipnis, PhD
Alan A. and Edith L. Wolff Distinguished Professor of Pathology and Immunology, Washington University at St. Louis
Dr. Jonathan (Jony) Kipnis is BJC Investigator, Alan A. and Edith L. Wolff Distinguished Professor of Pathology and Immunology and Professor of Neurology, Neuroscience, and Neurosurgery at Washington University in St. Louis, School of Medicine. He is also the inaugural Director of Brain immunology and Glia (BIG) Center at Washington University. Jony graduated from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, where he was Sir Charles Clore Scholar and a recipient of distinguished prize for scientific achievements awarded by the Israeli Parliament, The Knesset.
The Kipnis laboratory investigates the interactions between the immune system and the central nervous system, with a focus on the cellular and molecular mechanisms that govern brain function in health, aging, and neurological disease. His group demonstrated that normal brain function depends, in part, on an intact immune system and identified several cytokines as important neuromodulators. Most notably, his laboratory discovered the meningeal lymphatic vessels that drain the central nervous system into peripheral lymph nodes, revealing a direct anatomical link between the brain and the immune system. This finding reshaped the concept of central nervous system immune privilege and opened new avenues for studying neuroimmune interactions in health and disease, with implications for disorders including Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, autism, and age-related cognitive decline.
Dr. Kipnis is a member of National Academy of Medicine.

events.title: Cristopher Niell - Neural circuits for natural vision
events.abstract:
Join the speaker for coffee, cookies, and conversation before the talk, starting at 11:45am.
Neural circuits for natural vision
Abstract
Natural visual processing entails a complex interplay between sensory input, behavioral context, and on-going brain dynamics. Our lab seeks to understand how these processes give rise to goal-directed visual behaviors, by exploring the neural circuits mediating ethologically relevant behaviors that laboratory mice perform, including prey capture and distance estimation. We are also implementing novel experimental approaches to investigate neural coding of the visual scene as animals freely move through their environment. Finally, I will present a new research direction studying the completely different, yet largely unexplored, visual system of the octopus.In this work, we are elucidating both the functional and cell type organization to identify both shared and novel aspects of visual computation.
Cristopher Niell
University of Oregon
Cristopher Niell received his B.S. in physics at Stanford University, doing research in single-molecule biophysics with Dr. Steven Chu. He then remained at Stanford to obtain his PhD with Dr. Stephen Smith, studying the development and function of the zebrafish visual system. He then moved to UCSF to perform post-doctoral study with Dr. Michael Stryker, where he initiated studies of visual processing and behavioral state in the mouse cortex. He established his lab at University of Oregon in 2011, where he is now a Full Professor in the Department of Biology and Institute of Neuroscience. His lab uses a combination of neural recording and imaging methods, operant and ethological behaviors, and computational analysis to study the neural circuits that underlie visually guided behavior and perception.

events.abstract:
Jian Xiong
Knight Initiative Brain Resilience Postdoctoral Scholar, Stanford University
Abu-Remaileh Lab
Regulation of Bis(Monoacylglycero)Phosphate in Neurodegeneration
Bio & Abstract coming soon
Fei Deng
Postdoc, Stanford University
Owen Lab
Dynamic cholinergic modulation of cognitive function in Parkinson’s disease
Bio
Fei Deng is a postdoc in Scott Owen’s lab in the Neurosurgery Department. He is interested in neuromodulation and its applications to neurological diseases. He earned his Ph.D. from Peking University in 2023, where he developed genetically encoded serotonin sensors under the supervision of Professor Yulong Li. With a strong background in monitoring neuromodulators using advanced sensors and imaging techniques, he is dedicated to uncovering how neuromodulators shape complex brain functions and behaviors, currently focusing on the dynamics of acetylcholine signaling in the striatum during flexible learning and restorative interventions targeting the brain’s cholinergic system in Parkinson’s disease.
Abstract
The ability to adapt behavior in changing environments declines with normal aging and is further impaired in patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD). Dysregulated dopamine (DA) and acetylcholine (ACh) signaling in the striatum is thought to underline this deficit in flexible learning and represents an important therapeutic target. To uncover dynamics and functions of DA and ACh during flexible learning, I combined a two-spout licking task with dual-color fiber photometry recordings in healthy mice and a 6-OHDA model of PD. In healthy mice, unrewarded licking evoked a prominent rebound in ACh signaling. Strikingly, this ACh rebound was absent in the PD model, suggesting that it may play an important role in flexible learning. Indeed, pharmacological blockade of cholinergic signaling reduced both task engagement and switching ability, primarily through M4-type acetylcholine receptors. Dopamine depletion in the 6-OHDA PD model similarly impaired task performance, by reducing engagement and diminishing switching ability. Together, these findings identify dynamic cholinergic signaling as a key contributor to behavioral flexibility and suggest that restoring ACh modulation or its downstream signaling pathways may offer a strategy to alleviate PD-related cognitive decline while minimizing side effects.

events.title: Shagayeg Navabpour and Scott Dixon
events.abstract:
Shagayeg Navabpour
Postdoctoral Researcher, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Stanford University
Integrative Mental Health Laboratory (IMHL) [Duncan Lab]
From Genetic Risk to Brain Cell Types: Insights from Psychiatric and Neurodegenerative disorders
Bio
Shagayeg Navabpour is a Knight Initiative Brain Resilience Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford’s Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute, where she works with Dr. Laramie Duncan in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences.
She earned her BS in Biology and MS in Physiology from the University of Tehran, where she studied the endocannabinoid system in reward learning. After investigating genetic variation and brain structure in chimpanzees at Georgia State University, she completed her PhD in Translational Biology, Medicine, and Health at Virginia Tech with Dr. Timothy Jarome. Her doctoral research examined the molecular mechanisms of fear-memory formation, including epigenetic and chromatin dynamics and ubiquitin signaling.
Now working at the intersection of human genomics and single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics, Dr. Navabpour maps genetic risk for psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders onto specific human brain cell types. Across her experimental and computational work, she is guided by a central question: Why are particular brain cells, and particular individuals, vulnerable to disease while others remain resilient?
Shaghayegh has mentored undergraduate students at Stanford, Virginia Tech, and University of Tehran. She is also an actor and theater producer who explores the performing arts as a way to communicate neuroscience.
Abstract
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified many regions of the genome associated with brain disorders, but these findings do not directly reveal where in the brain genetic risk acts. Recent single-nucleus transcriptomic atlases provide an opportunity to connect genetic associations to the molecular profiles of precisely defined human brain cell types.
In this talk, Dr. Navabpour will describe an approach that integrates genome-wide association results with cell-type-specific gene expression across the human brain. Using psychiatric disorders as examples, she will show how this framework can move from broad genetic associations to specific neuronal populations and the brain regions in which they are found. She will then place these findings in the broader context of neurodegenerative disease. In Alzheimer’s disease, genetic risk points strongly toward microglia, highlighting the importance of non-neuronal immune mechanisms. In Parkinson’s disease, the strongest signals are concentrated among neuronal populations found primarily in the basal ganglia, as expected, but with newer brain atlases allowing these populations to be characterized at increasingly precise levels.
Together, these examples demonstrate how mapping genetic risk to specific human brain cell types can provide a biologically meaningful bridge from genetic risk to disease mechanism and help prioritize cellular systems for further investigation and opens up new avenues for better targeted therapeutic strategies.
Scott Dixon
Prof. Scott Dixon, Department of Biology, Stanford University
Dixon Lab
Regulation of non-apoptotic cell death by disease-associated genes in the endolysosomal network

As a postdoctoral fellow at Columbia University, he trained as a cell biologist and chemical biologist and helped discover the process of ferroptosis. His lab is currently focused on the regulation of non-apoptotic cell death in various disease contexts.

events.title: Eugene Wang: "Biocosmic Art; or How to Capture a Painter’s Brain?"
events.host_org: The Ho Center for Buddhist Studies
events.abstract:
Abstract:
When medical imaging mapped the neural deterioration of the legendary Hong Kong ink painter Irene Chou (1924-2011), she looked at her own brain X-rays and experienced a startling revelation: “I saw vital images of tree branches… that is life—my life.” In this lecture, Eugene Wang (Harvard University) reconsiders Chou’s art through the converging lenses of plant sensience, systems biology, and Buddhist-cum-Daoist meditative practice, revealing her paintings not as abstract landscapes but as experiments in biocosmic imagination. From the refuge of her father’s photographic darkroom in Shanghai to her solitary, obsessive sketches of “ten thousand trees” in Hong Kong’s dense woods, Chou turned ink into a means of self-preservation: thousands of rhythmic parallel lines became protective membranes, holding an endangered inner world against chaos. Bringing Charles Darwin’s studies of plant movement, Herbert Read’s modernist aesthetics, medical imaging, and the alchemical cosmology of breathing exercise into dialogue, Wang shows how Chou transformed illness and vulnerability into paintings of biocosmic imaginative reach—works that move from capillary and cell to vortex and galaxy, forging a radiant visual lexicon of resilience, renewal, and cosmic liberation.
Bio:
Eugene Y. Wang is the Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Professor of Asian Art at Harvard University. A Guggenheim Fellow and art-history editor of the Encyclopedia of Buddhism, he is the author of Shaping the Lotus Sutra: Buddhist Visual Culture in Medieval China, recipient of Japan’s Sakamoto Nichijin Academic Achievement Award.
Focused on the cognitive study of art, Wang’s research explores how images add up to function as worldmaking systems, and how art extends into biocosmic and psychocosmic dimensions. His work ranges from Asian Buddhist art and Chinese art history to immersive environments and digital media. He is the founding director of Harvard CAMLab, dedicated to the cognitive modeling of cultural systems.
In 2024, Wang curated Mawangdui: Art of Life, an immersive exhibition designed and produced by CAMLab that attracted more than one million visitors and received the 2025 iF Design Award in Germany. CAMLab’s Digital Gandhara was named a 2026 AWHEIC Star of Outstanding by a global heritage-education initiative of WHITRAP, a UNESCO Category 2 Centre. Wang is currently leading a new CAMLab project, Digital Borobudur.

events.title: 36th Annual Jonathan J. King Lecture: Dr. Bryant Lin & Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider
events.host_org: The Laurie J. Girand Center for Biomedical Ethics

events.abstract:
The Girand Center for Biomedical Ethics is pleased to announce this year’s speaker, Dr. Bryant Lin, in conversation with Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider, for the 36th Annual Jonathan J. King Lecture.
We invite you to join us on Thursday, November 5 at 5:30pm PT in the Cedar Room at the Stanford Faculty Club or via livestream for My Cancer Journey: Happiness and Sadness, Hope and Fear.
In this talk, Dr. Lin will share a candid and deeply personal reflection on living with terminal cancer. As a leading researcher, cancer advocate, and patient, he brings a rare perspective to the realities of serious illness, clinical care, hope, and what it means to live fully in the face of uncertainty. Joining Dr. Lin is Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider, a physician, journalist, producer, and leading voice in compassionate, patient-centered care. About the speakers
Bryant Lin, MD, MEng is a primary care physician, educator and researcher. The cornerstone of Dr. Lin's work is keeping medicine focused on humans - patients, providers, families and trainees - and not lost in technology and algorithms. His research and educational interests span (1) Developing and testing novel medical technologies, (2) Improving the health of Asian populations with Precision and Population Health, and (3) Increasing expression and interconnections in the Health Community with the Humanities and Arts. In 2018, he co-founded and currently co-directs, with Dr. Latha Palaniappan, the Center for Asian Health Research and Education (CARE) which aims to improve the health of Asians everywhere. events.title: Juan Gallego | More is different in neural populations
events.abstract:
Dr. Juan Gallego from the Champalimaud Foundation returns for the 2026–2027 MBCT Seminar Series
Join our mailing list for MBCT Seminar announcements and updates about future events
Abstract
Behaviour arises from interactions among regions and nuclei across the brain, each composed of a large number of interacting cells whose behaviour depends on complex interactions at the molecular level, and so on. The concept of emergence —“more is different”— says that new properties can arise from interactions among constituent parts that do not themselves have these properties. This most certainly applies to interactions among many brain regions, neurons, or molecules. Thus, the question arises: what level should we focus on if we want to understand how the brain generates behaviour?
In this talk, I will propose that the level of neural populations is appropriate to link specific brain functions to behavioural output. First, I will discuss evidence that studying the emergent properties of interacting neural populations leads to qualitatively new descriptions of brain function that are elusive when aggregating the individualistic behaviour of constituent neurons. Then, I will summarize evidence that the properties of this collective neural behaviour are not mere mathematical abstractions, but real patterns grounded in the biological substrates of the brain. I will end by discussing challenges and opportunities to further our understanding of brain function using this framework.
Continue the conversation: All attendees are invited to digest the seminar with a complimentary dinner with the speaker in the Theory Center after the seminar.

Juan Gallego, Principal Investigator, Champalimaud Foundation
Hosted by Yiqi Jiang (Schnitzer Lab & Linderman Lab)
Dr. Juan Gallego is a Principal Investigator at the Champalimaud Foundation, which he joined in October 2025. Prior to that, he was an Associate Professor at Imperial College London (since 2020), and held Postdoctoral Fellowships at the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) and Northwestern University. He was awarded a PhD from CSIC and University Carlos III in 2013.
Dr. Gallego’s research focuses on understanding how animals including humans acquire, execute and adapt their movements. To this end, his lab combines behavioural experiments in mice and humans, large-scale neural recordings, closed-loop manipulations, data analysis techniques, and computational models. He is also interested in applying his lab’s findings to advance neurotechnologies to restore function to people with movement disorders. During his career, he has published around fourty journal articles on these topics. His research has been funded by the EU Commission, the UK Research Institutes, ARIA, and the ERC.

Investigating preserved neural motifs across and within tasks in premotor cortex
Abstract
Motor systems neuroscience studies how populations of motor cortical neurons coordinate to perform motor computations, but less is known about how large repertoires of movements are flexibly generated from a fixed set of fundamental motor computations. There is an emerging idea of conserved neural “modules”, or recurring neural activity patterns deploying computations through dynamics, that may serve as elementary building blocks for performing the same fundamental computation across a wide array of contexts. However, exactly what feature of neural dynamics is “recurring” and fundamentally conserved, if any, when performing the same motor computation within a wide range of reach sequence and kinematic contexts has yet to be shown and characterized empirically.
To investigate this, we trained an animal implanted with a 96-channel Utah array in premotor cortex to perform 4 visually guided arm reaching motor tasks that are composed of unique combinations of 5 distinct motor processes (preparation, initiation, execution, hold, error correction) implemented in various reach conditions, where the same process can reappear across tasks and reappear again within tasks. This design allows us to test the hypothesis that premotor dynamics reuse conserved neural dynamics for performing the same motor computational process, but potentially implemented in different locations and orientations in population state space when reperformed across tasks, repeated in a sequence within tasks, and in different kinematic conditions. In this talk, I will explore systematically testing this hypothesis for all 5 motor processes to understand whether there are general organizing principles for premotor dynamics associated with deploying the same fundamental motor computation in a range of tasks, sequences, and kinematic contexts.
Meet the Speaker
Elizabeth Jun, PhD Student, Nuyujukian Lab, Stanford University
Elizabeth Jun is a neuroscience PhD Candidate at Stanford University and NIH F31 Predoctoral Fellow funded through National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS). Her research interests lie in understanding how large networks of neurons coordinate together to perform computations and support a wide range of behaviors in different contexts. Specifically in her thesis work, advised by Dr. Paul Nuyujukian in the Brain Interfacing Laboratory, she aims to understand how the brain can flexibly support a wide range of complex movements that are supported by a fixed set of fundamental motor computations. She is interested in connecting features of high-dimensional population data to similar behaviors in different contexts, and exploring in general how high-dimensional population features relate back to properties of the neural circuit.

events.title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Clive Neal - "Why the Moon Needs an International Lunar Resource Prospecting Campaign"
events.abstract:
The Moon is a highly valued destination for human space exploration because it is close and it contains a wide array of lunar and Solar System science targets, which include resources that could be used to sustain humans on the lunar surface. These resources have the potential to enable sustainable human space exploration, develop a vibrant cislunar economy, and directly benefit society here on Earth. However, recent rhetoric about the importance and value of these resources has used the term as if we know they are reserves. An immediate and vital next step has not yet been realized to define the reserve potential of such resources, and that is designing and implementing a coordinated international lunar resource evaluation (prospecting) campaign. This talk discusses the issues that still need to be addressed by such a campaign, including why it needs to be international in nature and how the coordination can be started and evolved, as well as exploring the benefits that would come from prospecting on the Moon.
Clive R. Neal is a lunar evangelist and Professor of Planetary Geology at the University of Notre Dame in Indiana, with 40 years of experience studying all aspects of the Moon and lunar exploration. He is passionate about establishing human permanence on the Moon in a way that benefits society here on Earth, while maximizing the scientific return that enables commercial involvement.
Neal has published over 150 peer-reviewed scientific articles and was a co-editor of the New Views of the Moon 1 and 2 volumes. He chaired NASA’s Lunar Exploration Analysis Group (LEAG) from 2006-2010, where he led the development of the U.S. Lunar Exploration Roadmap, and again from 2015-2018, when he formed the LEAG Commercial Advisory Board. In 2015, he received the NASA Wargo Award for the integration of exploration and planetary science throughout his career.
Neal was an advisor to the National Academies Committee on Astrobiology and Planetary Science (CAPS) from 2016 to 2017, and a member from 2018 to 2024. In 2019, he was invited to give testimony at the sixth meeting of the National Space Council regarding the importance of in-situ resource utilization. In 2025, Neal gave a technical presentation on lunar resource prospecting to the UN-COPUOS Legal Subcommittee; he gave another technical presentation to that subcommittee in 2026.
Also in 2026, Neal received two prestigious awards: NASA’s Eugene Shoemaker Distinguished Scientist Medal, which honors individuals who have made significant, career-spanning contributions to the field of lunar and planetary geoscience; and the AGU’s Waldo E. Smith Award, given biennially in even-numbered years to a senior scientist in recognition of extraordinary service to Earth and space science.

events.title: Geophysics Seminar - Allan Rubin, "Merging elastic/frictional and stochastic models of slow slip"
events.abstract:
Slow slip and nonvolcanic tremor were discovered over 20 years ago, but we still don’t understand how they are generated, or what distinguishes fault zones that produce slow slip from those that produce “regular” earthquakes. Models of slow slip tend to come in 2 flavors:
Continuum elastic/frictional models, designed to reproduce their slow propagation speeds and faster “tremor reversals”, and stochastic Brownian walk models, which lack basic physics but which reproduce various statistical properties of slow slip, including a ∼constant ratio of radiated seismic energy rate to moment rate. We have been exploring a stochastic elastic/frictional model that simultaneously reproduces many of the statistical properties of the stochastic models and the migration properties of continuum models. I’ll end by describing robust observations of tremor and slow slip that our model fails to reproduce, and
what this might tell us about processes acting in the slow slip source region.
Speaker-suggested reading:
Only up through section 3 of the following article: Xia, L., & Rubin, A. M. (2026). A simple discrete elastic model exhibits both the statistical properties and migration patterns of slow slip. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 131, e2026JB034106. https://doi.org/10.1029/2026JB034106

events.title: Geophysics Seminar - Shang-Ping Xie, "What powered the growth of 2026 super El Niño?"
events.abstract:
Speaker: Shang-Ping Xie
Distinguished Professor of Climate Science, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego
More information forthcoming
Abstract:
As early as March, the ECMWF and other climate forecast centers predicted a strong El Niño event for 2026—a forecast that has largely materialized, with Eastern Pacific sea surface temperature anomalies breaking century-long records. This super El Niño shares a distinctive two-part evolution common to the extreme El Niño events of 1982, 1997, and 2015. Specifically, the classic basin-scale El Niño driven by a deepened thermocline is preceded by a springtime (February–May) "booster" linked to the slow eastward expansion of the western Pacific warm pool coupled with westerly wind anomalies. The seminar presents real-time observations in relation to key El Niño precursors in the literature.
Speaker-suggested reading: Liang, Y., S.-P. Xie, A. Fedorov, Q. Peng, and A. Miyamoto, 2026: An eastward-propagating coupled mode amplifying the early growth of extreme El Niño events. Sci. Adv., 12, eaee0444. https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aee0444

events.location: Hewlett Teaching Center, 370 Jane Stanford Way, Stanford, CA 94305, 201
events.abstract:
Abstract: The Simons Observatory, a new millimeter-wave observatory in the Atacama, is now gathering data. With its smaller telescopes we are seeking a primordial signal imprinted by gravitational waves generated in the early universe. Its largest telescope is measuring the finer scales of the CMB with increased sensitivity, probing the initial conditions of the early universe as well as revealing the later-formed cosmic web of gas and dark matter through the gravitational lensing and Sunyaev Zel’dovich effects. It will map half the sky at arcminute resolution, overlapping with a number of large-scale structure surveys including Rubin. By surveying half the sky every couple of days, we also hope to see new types of transient astronomical events in millimeter-wavelengths. I will talk about the current status of SO, and its science plans.
Jo Dunkley is the Joseph Henry Professor of Physics and Astrophysical Sciences at Princeton University. She works on the analysis and interpretation of cosmological observations. She is currently the Spokesperson for the Simons Observatory collaboration. events.title: A Conversation with Researchers: Tracking HIV Through Wastewater in South Africa

The King Center on Global Development welcomes four visiting researchers from the South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC), working on HIV wastewater surveillance in KwaZulu-Natal.
A joint Stanford-SAMRC team is mapping HIV concentrations across northern KwaZulu-Natal to detect unrecognized transmission of HIV, measure changes in drug resistance and in anti-retroviral drug residues over time, enhance population surveillance, and track the success of interventions, offering a potentially cost-effective and relatively unbiased approach to public health monitoring.
Julie Parsonnet and Alexandra Boehm are co-Principal Investigators of the multiyear HIV Wastewater Epidemiology in South Africa Initiative.
Join Parsonnet and the SAMRC team for conversation over lunch, an opportunity to learn firsthand from African epidemiologists and laboratory scientists about the realities of their work in the field, and about infectious disease surveillance in vulnerable communities.
About the speakers:
Dr. Nomfundo Mahlangeni is a Senior Scientist at the SAMRC, where she leads the Water, Sanitation and Society Research Program within the Environment and Health Research Unit (EHRU). Her recent work includes detection and quantification of pharmaceutical compounds, including antiretroviral drugs, in wastewater. She is also passionate about research addressing the health and well-being of women and children in vulnerable communities.
Dr. Noluxabiso Mangwana is a Senior Scientist and epidemiologist at SAMRC’s Biomedical Research and Innovation Platform. Her research spans wastewater and environmental surveillance, antimicrobial resistance, and infectious disease epidemiology, integrating molecular tools and epidemiological analysis to inform public health action. Her current work includes infectious disease surveillance and the development of AMR surveillance within a One Health framework.
Nomacusi Sibeko is a Senior Research Technologist at SAMRC within the Environment and Health Research Unit (EHRU). Her research background includes microbiome–drug interactions, antimicrobial evaluations, and innovative approaches to water, urine, and faecal sludge treatment. In her current role, Sibeko is involved in environmental health research, particularly the wastewater-based surveillance of infectious diseases. She is passionate about applying laboratory science to address public health challenges.
Sthembile Sithole is a laboratory technician based at the University of Zululand, where she currently supports SAMRC on the Wastewater Surveillance of HIV RNA and Antiretroviral Drugs in KwaZulu-Natal, in collaboration with Stanford University. Her academic and research interests are focused on molecular and laboratory-based approaches to public health research, with particular interest in infectious disease surveillance and the application of wastewater epidemiology.
About the moderator:
Dr. Julie Parsonnet is a King Center faculty affiliate and Stanford Professor of Epidemiology and Population Health. Dr. Parsonnet is an Infectious Diseases clinician and epidemiologist whose research focuses on the role of infections in chronic disease. Her early work was pivotal in establishing H. pylori as a cause of gastric cancer and gastric lymphoma as well as protective effects of infections against esophageal diseases. About the Seminar:
As AI becomes woven into our daily lives and social institutions, we are becoming “cyborgs,” extending our minds and capabilities through technology. But greater technological capability does not automatically lead to greater human flourishing. How can we design AI that strengthens our ability to learn, create, connect, and make thoughtful decisions? In this talk, I will introduce an interdisciplinary approach to building AI systems and studying their effects on people. Through personalized AI prototypes and large-scale experiments, my research explores how AI can both enhance and undermine human decision-making, well-being, relationships, and sense of self. This work combines design, engineering, and qualitative and quantitative research to advance a science of human-AI interaction grounded in human flourishing. I will also explore how research can translate into real-world impact: from an AI digital twin that supports long-term thinking and has reached users in more than 100 countries, to research that has helped shape legislation protecting children from companion AI. Finally, I will discuss our efforts with collaborators across academia, industry, and government to develop the first open benchmark for AI’s impact on people. events.title: Distinguished Lecture Series| From Disentanglement to Re-Entanglement: Integrating the Living Archaeological Record
events.abstract:
Each quarter, the Stanford Archaeology Center invites prominent archaeologists from around the globe to be in residence for a week as a Distinguished Lecturer. During their residency, the Distinguished Lecturer gives two lectures and interacts with faculty, postdoctoral scholars and students. Stanford Archaeology Center will host Prof. Christopher H. Roosevelt from Koc University over two days (Feb 24 and Feb 25 for the Winter Quarter of this academic year.
Abstract:
Recent trends in archaeological data management have focused on preserving, linking, comparing, and reusing datasets, and rightly so. The expensive work of archaeological practice is too often relegated to inaccessible files and legacy databases, recoverable only when future opportunities afford revived engagement. While legacy datasets are one clear challenge, so too are living datasets, those still growing, still under analysis. As archaeological practice is increasingly specialized, its domain-specific archives have increasing difficulty speaking to one another. Ceramics, small finds, botanical and faunal remains, conservation records, drawings, photographs, and spatial data accumulate in parallel systems that share an archaeological site but can otherwise become siloed. This happens to born-digital projects too. The Kaymakçı Archaeological Project (KAP) was born digital in 2014; by 2026 its records were accessed across seventeen separate database forms, on their way to legacy status.
This lecture presents KAPDash for the first time: an integrated research platform, built in five months and still growing, that reunites twelve seasons of textual, spatial, image, and laboratory data and the specialists who produce them in a single interlinked system. Its organization follows archaeology’s own domains rather than software conventions, a consequence of its development by an archaeologist working with AI assistance rather than by software engineers. That same organization allows anyone on the project, specialist or not, to browse connected datasets intuitively, ask questions of the whole record in natural language, and see not only answers but the queries that produced them. Excavation destroys contextual relations, and specialization can result in further data disentanglement. KAPDash demonstrates a means of re-entangling the archaeological record and providing broad access, enabling holistic analysis and interpretation.

events.title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Catherine Johnson - "Mercury’s Enigmatic Magnetic Field"
events.abstract:
Mercury’s interior structure and its magnetic field are unique among the terrestrial planets and moons of the Solar System. Its large metallic core (~83% of the planetary radius) formed under highly reducing conditions, requiring a core composition that includes substantial silicon and some, but more limited, sulfur and carbon. Mercury is also the only planet other than Earth to have both core and crustal magnetic fields. The core field constrains the present-day dynamo and crustal magnetization, if remanent, can constrain the dynamo history. The core field is dominantly dipolar, axisymmetric, asymmetric about the planetary equator, and ~100 times weaker than Earth’s field at the planetary surface. Structure beyond this simple picture is weak but exists, in particular a high-northern-latitude regional magnetic field anomaly spatially coincident with the topographic and gravity signature of Mercury’s Northern Rise. Crustal fields in many places can be explained by magnetizations induced in the present field and thus are a probe of the magnetic properties of the crust rather than the dynamo history. However, stronger magnetizations at some craters and basins are consistent with the existence of a dynamo at the time of formation of the Caloris Basin and more recently, with the caveat that impactor-delivered iron could also contribute to enhanced induced magnetizations. These magnetic field constraints must collectively be matched by dynamo models: how does the thermal state and precise core composition (e.g., the relative amounts of Si, S, and C) control the solidification history of the inner core, and the radial extent of dynamo region(s) in the outer core? To what extent do core-mantle interactions, physical or chemical, affect core dynamics now and in the past? I will discuss how upcoming BepiColombo data can address some of these open questions
Catherine Johnson is a Professor at the University of British Columbia and a Senior Scientist at the Planetary Science Institute. Her research focuses on understanding the structure and interior evolution of terrestrial planets, moons and asteroids. She is a Guest Investigator on the Bepi-Colombo mission and was previously a Participating Scientist on the MESSENGER (Mercury) mission, and a Co-Investigator on the InSight (Mars) and OSIRIS-REx (asteroid Bennu) missions. She is a member of the U. S. National Academy of Sciences, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and a fellow of the Royal Society of Canada and the AGU. Beyond geophysics she enjoys being outside, cooking and eating good food with excellent company, her local community sewing studio, and teaching yoga.
Speaker suggested reading: Johnson, C. L., Plattner, A. M., Cicchetti, F., & Miljković, K. (2026). The distribution and origin of Mercury's crustal magnetization. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(35), e2535723123. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2535723123

events.title: CEE PhD Defense: Gustavo A. Araújo Rodríguez, "Heterogenous CPU–GPU Parallel Computing for Real-Time Hybrid Simulation"
events.abstract:
Abstract:
Real-time hybrid simulation (RTHS) combines physical experimentation with numerical simulation to investigate the dynamic response of complex engineering systems. However, the fidelity and complexity of the numerical models used in RTHS are constrained by the computational demands of solving the governing equations in real time. Consequently, numerical models in RTHS are often limited in size (e.g., fewer than 1,000 degrees of freedom) and rely on simplified representations of complex physical phenomena, such as soil–structure interaction (SSI). This dissertation investigates heterogeneous CPU–GPU parallel computing to expand the computational capabilities of RTHS within the open-source OpenSees framework. The proposed architecture distributes element and constitutive state determination across CPU processes while accelerating the solution of the assembled system and the numerical integration of the equations of motion on a GPU. Existing GPU-accelerated direct and iterative solvers are integrated through interchangeable backends, together with a Python-delegated interface for external solver libraries. The computational performance of these implementations is evaluated using structural and soil--structure interaction models ranging from thousands to hundreds of thousands of degrees of freedom. To enable computationally efficient time integration, the model-based modified Kolay–Ricles-alpha (MKR-alpha) integration method is reformulated for CPU-parallelized and GPU-accelerated execution. The resulting computational framework is demonstrated through hydrodynamic RTHS of a soil–foundation–bridge system subjected to sequential earthquake and wave loading at the Large Wave Flume facility at Oregon State University. The numerical model explicitly represented nonlinear SSI using continuum finite elements, avoiding the simplified SSI representations often adopted to meet the computational constraints of RTHS. A model with more than 2,000 degrees of freedom satisfied hard real-time constraints, while models containing approximately 4,000–5,500 degrees of freedom achieved soft real-time performance. Beyond RTHS applications, the implemented framework achieved computational speedups in nonlinear dynamic analyses of models containing hundreds of thousands of degrees of freedom. These findings demonstrate the potential of heterogeneous CPU–GPU parallel computing to enable higher-fidelity numerical modeling in RTHS and expand the computational capacity for large-scale nonlinear dynamic analysis.
