events.title: ESE Seminar - Eva Schill: "Potential for Lithium and Other Critical Mineral Extraction from Geothermal Waters and Brines in the US"
events.abstract:
Abstract
Lithium-bearing brines offer the United States an opportunity to co-produce critical minerals and geothermal energy. Realizing this potential requires a better understanding of brine chemistry, reservoir dynamics, and the long-term sustainability of lithium extraction.
The Salton Sea geothermal field in California is a distinctive setting for lithium–geothermal co-production. Since 2004, geothermal brine production has averaged just over 120 million metric tons per year. At an estimated lithium concentration of 198 mg/L, this brine contains approximately 127,000 metric tons of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) annually. The estimated lithium inventory in the well-characterized portion of the field is 4.1 million metric tons LCE. However, estimates that account for geophysical data on reservoir extent and revised assumptions about porosity suggest that the broader Lithium Valley resource could contain as much as 18 million metric tons LCE (Kaspereit et al., 2016; Dobson et al., 2023). As direct lithium extraction advances, sustained production will depend in part on replenishment from deeper, convecting brines and lithium-bearing minerals in the surrounding reservoir. Fluid circulation and recharge, the chemistry and reactivity of deeper lithium-bearing minerals, and reinjection strategies may affect long-term recovery.
The Jurassic Smackover Formation, extending along the Gulf Coast from Texas to Florida, also contains some of the highest-lithium produced waters in the United States, with concentrations exceeding 500 mg/L in southern Arkansas. Concentrations in low-temperature thermal waters in Texas, Mississippi, and Alabama are generally lower but locally exceed 300 mg/L. Previous studies have associated Smackover lithium concentrations with H₂S levels, reservoir depth and thickness, water–rock interaction, and major faults. Our analysis of the U.S. Geological Survey’s National Produced Waters Geochemical Database supports an evaporitic origin for lithium and identifies substantial magnesium, which may need to be removed before lithium extraction. We are also investigating the role of clay minerals in the system. Together, these studies will inform extraction-process design and assessment of the potential to recover multiple critical elements, while improving understanding of the economic potential and long-term sustainability of domestic brine resources.
Bio
Eva Schill is a Staff Scientist in the Geophysics Department of Berkeley Lab’s Earth and Environmental Sciences Area (EESA) where she serves as the Lead of the Geothermal Systems Program of the Energy and Geoscience Division. At the Technical University of Darmstadt, Germany, Dr. Schill is Professor for Geophysics in Reservoir Systems. She obtained her Ph.D. from the Eberhard Karls University in Tübingen in Germany. After her postdoctoral research at ETH Zürich, Switzerland and Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, Germany, where she was appointed first Junior Professor for Geothermics. After serving as Professor for Geothermics at the University of Neuchâtel, Switzerland, she was a leading scientist at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Germany, before joining LBNL. Dr. Schil is a geologist and geophysicist and deals with geothermal issues from exploration to reservoir behavior. She combines various geological and geophysical methods to understand the structure of the subsurface. In combination with hydromechanical experiments, Dr. Schill is developing new monitoring methods that go beyond the monitoring of induced seismicity and shed light on reservoir processes. She is also working on new technologies to mitigate induced seismicity.

events.title: Earth & Planetary Sciences Seminar - Prof. Benjamin Gill "Exploring the potential links between ocean oxygenation and the evolution of early Paleozoic marine ecosystems"
events.abstract:
Abstract: The beginning of the Phanerozoic saw two major diversification events in the history of life on our planet: the Cambrian Explosion (~530 to 510 Ma) and the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event (~471 to 458 Ma), or GOBE. These two events are separated by a plateau diversity that spanned from the later Cambrian and Early Ordovician, roughly ~40 million years. On a finer temporal scale, the fossil record shows that this diversity plateau contains at least six rapid turnover events in the marine fauna: extinction events followed by rapid diversifications. The causes of this repetitive turnover in marine ecosystems remain an open question and was likely were driven by several environmental and biological factors.
Numerous lines of geochemical and mineralogical evidence indicate that the later Cambrian and Early Ordovician oceans were persistently less oxygenated than todays. Additionally, marine redox chemistry also varied considerably in conjunction with the biological turnover events. One of these events, the end-Marjuman extinction (~494 Ma), is by far the most well-studied in this regard. This interval was marked by perturbations in the global carbon and sulfur cycles, reflected by positive excursions in the marine carbon and sulfur isotope records referred to as the Steptoean Positive Carbon Isotope Excursion or SPICE. Extensive work, relying on multiple lines of evidence has linked these carbon and sulfur cycle perturbations to an interval of marine deoxygenation. Our work on three of the other extinction events has revealed both similar and dissimilar geochemical records to those of the SPICE, despite the similarity in the changes in marine communities across the events. However, all these events appear to coincide with evidence for declines in marine oxygenation. Therefore, the pause in building marine diversity in the early Paleozoic was in part both directly and in directly tied sustained low and variable marine oxygen levels.
Speaker Bio: I spent my childhood growing up in the Midwest of the United States, mostly in Wisconsin and Missouri. I received my bachelor’s degree in Geological Sciences from the University of Missouri in 2004 and my PhD in Earth Sciences from the University of California Riverside 2009. from 2009-2011, I was a postdoctoral researcher at Harvard. I have been a professor in the Department of Geoscience at Virginia Tech since 2012. My research interests concern evolution of biogeochemical cycles, the interplay of life and the environment across Earth history, and the novel application of stable isotopes to scientific problems. I outside of work I enjoy distance running, gardening, and camping with my family.

events.title: Wormholes and the Conformal Bootstrap
events.location: Hewlett Teaching Center, 370 Jane Stanford Way, Stanford, CA 94305, 201
events.abstract:
Abstract: A wormhole is a geometry which connects two widely separated regions of space-time. Wormholes are ubiquitous in many theories of gravity, but remain poorly understood. However, we can study them using the "AdS/CFT correspondence," which relates theories of quantum gravity to conformal field theories (CFTs) in one less dimension. These CFTs are similar to the gauge theories which describe the fundamental forces of particle physics, as well as to those which describe important statistical and condensed matter systems at criticality. I will describe a simple setup where we can understand the effects of wormholes precisely, using a set of strongly coupled techniques known as the conformal bootstrap. We will conclude that Einstein gravity is described by to a “disorder averaged” quantum theory, much like a spin glass or other system with quantum chaos. The upshot is this: in a theory of gravity with wormholes, the coupling constants of nature look like random variables.
Alexander Maloney is a theoretical physicist working on problems in quantum field theory and quantum gravity. His primary interests include questions related to the quantum structure of space-time, and in particular the entropy and thermodynamics of black holes. He has made important contributions to the study of conformal field theories, particularly those in two dimensions, and in the interplay between the dynamics of strongly coupled field theories and theories of gravity. He has played an important role in the use of quantum information theoretic methods in quantum field theories and quantum gravity. Maloney received a B.Sc. in physics and an M.Sc. in mathematics from Stanford University in 1998, and a Ph.D. in physics from Harvard University in 2003. This was followed by postdoctoral positions at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center and the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. He joined the faculty of McGill University in 2007, where he was a James McGill professor and Sir William Macdonald Chair in Physics. In 2024 he moved to Syracuse University, where is the Kathy and Stan Walters Endowed Professor of Quantum Science and director of the Institute for Quantum and Information Sciences

events.title: Geophysics PhD Defense, Becca Prentice: "Utilizing Transient Electromagnetic Method to Locate Pathways for River-Sourced Recharge in the San Joaquin Valley"
events.location: Mitchell Earth Sciences, Hartley Conference Center
events.abstract: The importance of water is becoming increasingly apparent across the globe. As more regions experience swings in climate, from extreme dry periods to extreme wet periods, there is growing recognition of the importance of storing excess water during wet periods for use during dry periods. Storing water beneath the ground provides an alternative to reservoirs, which do not always provide sufficient storage and are expensive to build, with associated environmental impacts. Recharging groundwater systems has become a key solution for restoring groundwater levels and increasing water storage, and natural recharge needs to be protected and increased for the sustainable management of groundwater. The goal of this thesis is to locate river-sourced recharge pathways in California’s San Joaquin Valley. I leveraged two geophysical methods, both based on the transient electromagnetic method, one airborne and one ground-based, to map the distribution of sediment types in the subsurface, which is needed to identify pathways for river-sourced recharge.

events.title: Geophysics PhD Defense, Danny May: "Exploration Geophysics-Inspired Acquisition and Analysis for Ice-Penetrating Radar"
events.abstract:
Radio-echo sounding of ice sheets provides key constraints on englacial and subglacial material and thermal conditions. However, standard survey configurations have made it difficult to unambiguously resolve properties such as fine-scale bed geometry, ice temperature, and subglacial hydrological conditions and to monitor how these properties evolve over time. This work presents a set of low-cost modifications to existing radar systems (using radio frequency-over-fiber) that help address these limitations by enabling larger distributed antenna arrays and greater sensor separations than are conventionally possible.
Results are presented from several field deployments illustrating the range of applications this enables. A large imaging array deployed on a polythermal glacier in Svalbard resolves the ice-bed interface with much improved resolution compared to standard stationary configurations. Polarimetric surveys collected at large offsets in Antarctica probe englacial dielectric and thermal structure. Finally, survey geometries adapted from exploration seismology, including a towed antenna array, a borehole sensor, and a stationary array operated over multiple days, were deployed on a temperate glacier in Alaska to recover near-surface properties and their evolution over time. Together, these results improve the ability to constrain material properties and monitor glacier processes over time, forming the foundation for 3D time-lapse imaging of ice sheet structure.

events.title: Christopher Ong | Research Acceleration: The View Inside OpenAI
events.abstract:
In the last year, AI models have rapidly improved on public benchmarks measuring their ability to carry out research tasks autonomously. Such performance suggests that models may be capable of automating parts of the AI R&D process itself, thereby accelerating the pace of AI progress. However, there is still little empirical data on how these new capabilities have changed the research process within the AI labs at the research frontier. This talk will share findings from OpenAI's recent report on AI-powered research acceleration, which aims to help fill this gap. We will also discuss future research directions for the economics of recursive self-improvement (RSI).
The report documents several stylized facts. First, models are increasingly capable of autonomously completing research tasks that would take a human researcher several hours or even days to finish. However, completing longer tasks remains challenging and more frequently requires human intervention. Second, agentic use is rapidly increasing, such that total hours worked by the agent workforce is several times that of the human workforce. Finally, researchers intensely use agents for execution-oriented tasks such as writing code, reviewing technical work, and managing training runs, but high-level planning remains primarily bottlenecked on humans.

events.title: PhD Dissertation Defense: Danielle Klinger
events.abstract:
Title: Non-Destructive Contractility Measurements on Developing Cardioids
Abstract: The force generated by the heart depends in part on how much the cardiac muscle is stretched, and diseases that disrupt this mechanical function, are a major cause of heart failure. Cardioids are 3D engineered heart tissues, derived from human stem cells, that beat spontaneously and reproduce features of the developing heart, making them promising models for studying disease and testing drugs. However, measuring their mechanical function without disrupting the tissue remains challenging. In this work, I developed a non-destructive compression assay to measure contractile force and passive stiffness in intact cardioids. First, I applied it to track individual cardioids throughout maturation and showed that they become smaller, generate more force, and perform more mechanical work with each beat as they mature, similar to the developing human heart. Second, I demonstrated that cardioids exhibit a Frank-Starling response, the increase in contractile force with stretch, that helps the heart adapt to changing demands, and that this response strengthened with maturation. Third, I showed that the cardiac myosin inhibitor mavacamten suppresses this response in a dose-dependent manner. Finally, I applied the assay to a patient-derived model of restrictive cardiomyopathy and found greater contractile force and sensitivity to stretch compared with genetically corrected controls. Together, this work establishes a method for repeatedly measuring the mechanical function of intact human cardiac organoids, enabling studies of cardiac development, drug responses, and disease.

events.title: ESE Seminar - Bo Guo: "Fate and Transport of PFAS in Unsaturated Porous Media across Scales: Interfacial Partitioning, Thin Water Films, and Upscaling"
events.abstract:
Abstract
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are contaminants that have accumulated extensively in soils, which can act as long-term sources of groundwater contamination. Quantifying soil PFAS leaching is therefore critical for risk assessment, remediation, and regulatory decision-making. However, PFAS transport differs fundamentally from that of conventional contaminants because many PFAS are surfactants that adsorb at air–water and solid–water interfaces, leading to complex retention behavior and flow–transport coupling under variably saturated conditions.
I present a cross-scale framework for understanding and modeling PFAS fate and transport in soils and groundwater. I discuss the dominant processes controlling PFAS retention and migration, introduce a mechanistic mathematical model that incorporates PFAS-specific interfacial processes, and show how thin water films can uniquely control PFAS transport in unsaturated soils. This is followed by a multi-continuum, semi-analytical framework as a potential route for upscaling these processes and incorporating them into practical modeling tools. The goal is to connect interfacial physics across scales to improve predictions of long-term PFAS retention, leaching, and mass discharge to groundwater.
Bio
Dr. Bo Guo is an Associate Professor and University Distinguished Scholar at the University of Arizona. His research focuses on fluid flow and transport in porous media, with an emphasis on multiscale mathematical and computational modeling. He works on a range of environmental and energy problems, including contaminant transport in soils and groundwater, chemical weathering in the critical zone, shale oil and gas production, and geologic carbon storage. Bo earned his B.S. (with highest honor) from Tsinghua University and Ph.D. from Princeton University, and completed a two-year postdoc at Stanford University before joining the University of Arizona. He is the 2027 Henry Darcy Distinguished Lecturer, and a recipient of the AGU Hydrologic Sciences Early Career Award, NSF CAREER Award, and the Humboldt Research Fellowship for Experienced Researchers. He serves as an Editor of Hydrology and Earth System Sciences and an Associate Editor of Water Resources Research, and Advances in Water Resources.

Abstract: Quantum processors and simulators now probe the dynamics of hundreds of quantum constituents in regimes that challenge classical algorithms. These advances open unprecedented opportunities to explore quantum matter while raising a fundamental question: when do quantum simulations of many-body systems offer a meaningful computational advantage over classical methods? In this colloquium, I will describe recent experiments using superconducting analog and digital processors to prepare correlated low-energy states and probe their interacting quasiparticles. I will then discuss theoretical insights into the complexity of simulating many-body dynamics, showing how they inspire new classical algorithms while guiding the future applications of quantum processors.
Dmitry Abanin is Professor of Physics who joined the Princeton faculty in August of 2023. He received his Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 2008. His scientific interests and areas of study include quantum simulation, quantum information and computing, condensed matter physics, and efficient classical algorithms for quantum systems. He has published over ninety peer-reviewed papers and has received numerous awards, including the recent Clarivate Highly Cited Researcher Award in 2023 and the ERC Consolidator Grant in 2020. He is currently on the graduate admissions committee for the new graduate program in Quantum Science and Engineering, which is a joint collaboration between the Physics and Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) Departments.

Beyond Blood: Transplant and Gene-Edited Cell Therapy for Neurodegenerative Disease in Children
PRESENTER:
Natalia Gomez-Ospina, MD, PhD
Assistant Professor of Pediatrics, Medical Genetics
Stanford School of Medicine
SESSION DESCRIPTION
Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is standard of care for a small number of neurodegenerative inherited disorders — metachromatic leukodystrophy, Krabbe disease, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, and severe MPS type 1 — yet outcomes remain disappointing for most patients. Donor-derived cells repopulate the CNS slowly and incompletely, so neurologic decline often outpaces engraftment, while myeloablative conditioning and graft-versus-host disease impose morbidity that narrows the risk-benefit window. With newborn screening now detecting many of these disorders before symptom onset, the principal constraint on outcomes is no longer early diagnosis but the limitations of available therapy. This session reviews two developments that may substantially improve outcomes for these patients. The first is a conditioning strategy that pairs brain-penetrant chemotherapy with transient CSF1R inhibition, which in preclinical models achieves near-complete microglial replacement within weeks rather than months. The second is autologous transplantation of hematopoietic stem cells gene-edited at the CCR5 safe harbor to secrete supraphysiologic enzyme, eliminating the need for a matched donor and the risk of GVHD. Data will be presented across MPS type 1, Gaucher disease, and Friedreich’s ataxia, including evidence that engrafted myeloid cells benefit surrounding tissue not only through enzyme cross-correction but also by transferring intact mitochondria, with improvements in both neurologic and cardiac endpoints. The session closes with the manufacturing, genotoxicity, and regulatory requirements that stand between these results and first-in-human trials.
EDUCATION GOALS
Describe the current indications for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in inherited neurodegenerative disease and the clinical factors — delayed CNS engraftment, conditioning-related toxicity, and graft-versus-host disease — that limit its benefit in rapidly progressive disorders.
Differentiate the mechanisms by which engrafted donor myeloid cells correct disease in the CNS and other tissues, and apply this understanding to anticipate which disorders and which patients are most likely to benefit.
Assess the preclinical efficacy and safety evidence for autologous hematopoietic stem cell products in lysosomal storage disorders, and identify their implications for patient counseling, timing of referral, and future trial eligibility.

events.title: Sustainable Systems Seminar Lunch Series - Hierarchical Solving of High-Resolution Energy System Models
events.abstract:
This week's speaker is:
Andreas Mühlbauer, Leavell Fellow and PhD student, Stanford University
"Hierarchical Solving of High-Resolution Energy System Models"
Abstract:
Energy system models that plan highly renewable systems need high resolution in space and time. US grid operators schedule power in 15-minute intervals and dispatch real-time markets every 5 minutes. At such time steps, a full year of a large network quickly becomes too large to solve, so models are coarsened once and their error is rarely known. This talk presents a hierarchical approach similar to the nested grids of weather and climate models: a coarse model of the whole year and system is solved first, and its results serve as boundary conditions for finer levels that are solved in parallel time windows. We test the approach in PyPSA on standard IEEE networks with 14 to 118 buses, which are small enough to solve in full, so every gap to the optimum is exact. At 15-minute resolution, the hierarchy is 2.8–4.0 times faster on the same cores and stays within 0.45–0.9% of the optimum. I close with an outlook on bridging continental and local scales, using the example of zooming into US metropolitan areas.
Bio:
Andreas Mühlbauer is a Leavell Fellow and PhD student in Civil and Environmental Engineering at Stanford University, where he develops optimization frameworks for multi-sector energy systems. His research covers a range of topics in energy system transitions, including renewable integration, infrastructure planning, wind repowering, and carbon management. His current work focuses on renewable microgrids and on hierarchical methods for solving high-resolution energy system models.
Before Stanford, Andreas gained research experience at the Lappeenranta-Lahti University of Technology (Finland), the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (Germany), and the non-profit Energy Watch Group (Germany), working at the intersection of renewable energy modeling, carbon management technologies, and climate policy.
The topics of this seminar are broad but typically fall under technologies’ scaling potential and impact on (the system of) people, the environment and the economy. A particular focus is placed on the interaction potential of technologies with the energy, water, and material systems. Our goal is to create an intimate, collaborative space for students, postdocs, scientists, and PIs within Stanford across micro-level (material and technology) to macro-level (system) interests. These seminars will provide an opportunity to disseminate insights from your studies, connect with fellow researchers, and strengthen bonds across the community.

events.title: Earth & Planetary Sciences Seminar - Dr. Sarah Lambart "From Basalt Chemistry to Mantle Mineralogy: Understanding Magmatism from Intraplate Volcanism to Continental Breakup"
events.abstract:
Abstract: Basaltic rocks provide a window into the Earth's mantle, recording information about the rocks that melt at depth and the processes that bring magma to the surface. But how much can we really learn about the mantle from basalt chemistry? In this seminar, I will first introduce BaSIC (Basalt Source Investigation and Characterization), a new open-source tool that uses the chemical composition of basalts to estimate the mineralogy of their mantle sources . Applying BaSIC to ocean island basalts reveals how tectonic setting and lithospheric thickness influence which mantle components contribute to melting. I will then show how we can use such tool to investigate the cause of magmatism during continental breakup, focusing on the opening of the Northeast Atlantic around 56 million years ago. Our results show that changes in mantle source mineralogy accompanied variations in magmatic activity, and suggest that thinning of the lithosphere, rather than high mantle temperatures alone, was a major driver of this magmatism.
Bio: Dr. Sarah Lambart is an Associate Professor in the Department of Geology and Geophysics at the University of Utah. Her primary research focuses on the chemistry of Earth and planetary interiors with a particular emphasis on the role of magma generation and magma-rock interaction on the differentiation and chemical evolution of terrestrial planets. She combines experimental techniques, high temperature geochemistry and thermodynamical modeling to investigate a range of various processes from magma focusing in the asthenosphere to formation of ore deposits. Dr Lambart earned her MS and PhD at Blaise Pascal University in France and had postdoctoral appointments at Caltech, Columbia University, UC Davis, and Cardiff University in Wales. She joined University of Utah in 2018.

events.abstract:
EARTH SYSTEM SCIENCE

Y2E2, Room 299
Jenan Kharbush, Ph.D.
Assistant Professor
University of Michigan
“A moving nitrogen target: How nitrogen availability and speciation shape the ecology of Microcystis-dominated cyanobacterial blooms”
Abstract
In cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (CyanoHABs) dominated by the non-diazotrophic cyanobacterium Microcystis, nitrogen availability is critical for production of the nitrogen-rich toxin microcystin, and may also play a role in shaping Microcystis strain composition and relative abundance of toxic and non-toxic strains. During the annual CyanoHAB in Western Lake Erie, the dominant nitrogen pools shift between inorganic and organic forms as the bloom progresses. At the same time, Microcystis strain composition and the heterotrophic bacterial communities associated with Microcystis colonies also change. Recent metagenomics and culture-based work suggests that some of these heterotrophs participate in nitrogen acquisition and cycling processes with Microcystis. In this talk, I will discuss our efforts to understand the influence of nitrogen availability and speciation on Microcystis bloom ecology using nano-secondary ion mass spectrometry (nanoSIMS), complemented by shotgun metagenomic and transcriptomic community data. Our results suggest that Microcystis maintains a broad capacity to assimilate multiple nitrogen substrates across all bloom phases, effectively remaining primed to exploit shifting nitrogen pools regardless of their ambient concentrations. This flexibility may help sustain Microcystis dominance under changing bloom conditions.
Biography
I am an Assistant Professor in the Earth and Environmental Sciences Department at the University of Michigan. I earned my PhD in Chemical Oceanography from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography in San Diego, CA, where I first developed an appreciation for the complexity of microbial life and the outsized impacts microbes have on their environment. At U-M, my research group studies how aquatic microorganisms, particularly phytoplankton, acquire and use nitrogen, including during cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms. The lab combines laboratory culture experiments with field-based environmental observations to link cellular-level nitrogen cycling processes to large-scale geochemical patterns in both modern and ancient environments.

Clothing is a complex and sensitive record of history—evincing the interplay of culture, technology, and artistry. At the same time, textile goods are notoriously difficult to conserve and display; in this context, paper sewing patterns provide a valuable record of historical clothing and methods of clothing manufacture. Our project, “Pattern Magic,” aims to dramatically improve the quantity and quality of historical garments available for research and creative use by (1) creating a database of 3D garments reconstructed from 60K historical patterns (earliest from the 1850s) available in the Commercial Pattern Archive (held at the University of Rhode Island) and (2) developing user-friendly tools which allow individuals and libraries to use our methods to contribute to this or other databases.

events.abstract:
Abstract: In humans’ immune response, B cells that produce high-affinity (strongly binding) antibodies are generated through a Darwinian evolutionary process called “affinity maturation”. Affinity maturation, which takes place in germinal centers (GCs), is driven by cycles of selection (mediated by T cells), division, and hypermutation of B cells. Recently, it was found that the T cells themselves also exhibit dynamic behavior throughout the course of the GC reaction, undergoing affinity-dependent proliferation. A model suggests that this reciprocal stimulation enforces a robust “homeostatic” regulation of the relative number of B cells and T cells in the GC, leading to a constant ratio of T cells to B cells. But the model also points to a problem: the high mutation rate of GC B cells can lead to “backsliding” of affinity. The proposed solution – a fitness-dependent mutation rate – has been experimentally verified, and has implications beyond B cell affinity maturation.
Ned Wingreen is the Howard A. Prior Professor of the Life Sciences at Princeton University. He is a member of the Department of Molecular Biology and Associate Director of the Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics, where he is Director of Graduate Studies of the QCB Graduate Program. He is also associated faculty in the Department of Physics. Ned received his Ph.D. in theoretical condensed matter physics from Cornell University in 1989. He did his postdoc in mesoscopic physics at MIT before moving, in 1991, to the NEC Research Institute in Princeton. At NEC, he continued to work in mesoscopic physics, but also started research in biophysics which grew into a general interest in problems at the interface of physics and biology. Ned joined Princeton University in 2004. Ned's current research focuses on modeling of bacteria, bacterial communities, phages, and other microorganisms, as well as studies of intracellular phase separation, and topics in immunology. He is a fellow of the American Physical Society and the American Association for the Advancement of Science.

events.title: Earth & Planetary Sciences Seminar - Prof. Peng Ni "Unraveling Earth’s dynamic history through sublithospheric diamonds"
events.abstract:
Abstract: Most natural diamonds form at depths of 120 to 200 km in Earth’s lithospheric mantle. A small fraction, however, originates much deeper. This group of diamonds, known as sublithospheric diamonds, includes some of the largest and finest diamonds in the world. These diamonds can contain mineral inclusions that represent some of the deepest samples of Earth’s interior. In this talk, I will show how the chemistry of these inclusions records the geological history experienced by their host diamonds, providing a unique window into the dynamic processes that have shaped our planet over time.
Speaker Bio: Peng Ni is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Earth, Planetary, and Space Sciences at the University of California, Los Angeles. His research focuses on understanding the large-scale geochemical processes that have shaped Earth, Moon, and other terrestrial bodies throughout their formation, differentiation, and evolution. His group combines a wide range of approaches, including non-traditional stable isotope geochemistry, high-pressure high-temperature experiments, studies of natural sample studies, and geochemical modeling. His recent work includes investigating the recycling of surface materials into Earth’s deep interior using diamond inclusions; studying Apollo samples to better understand the Moon’s volatile budget and volcanic activity; and experimentally constraining the behavior of moderately volatile elements during evaporation processes.

events.title: New frontier of Quantum Computing
events.location: Hewlett Teaching Center, 370 Jane Stanford Way, Stanford, CA 94305, 201
events.abstract:
A broad effort is currently underway to develop quantum computers that can outperform classical counterparts for certain computational, simulation or sensing tasks. The practical realization of such systems and exploration of their potential capabilities and limitations are central themes in the new field of quantum science and engineering. A central challenge in quantum computing is error suppression, which requires quantum error correction for large-scale processing. However, the overhead involved in creating error-corrected "logical" qubits-where information is redundantly encoded across multiple physical qubits-presents a significant obstacle to scalable quantum computing. In this talk, we will discuss recent advances in the programmable, coherent manipulation of quantum systems using neutral atom arrays excited into Rydberg states. These advances allow control over several hundred qubits and the exploration of quantum algorithms with encoded logical qubits and quantum error correction techniques. Enabled by the remarkable interdisciplinary effort, involving academia and industry, these advances have redefined the frontier of quantum computing and quantum information. They herald the advent of early error-corrected quantum computation, paving the way for new applications and inspiring a shift in addressing both the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead. Several examples of emerging applications, ranging from quantum many-body physics to quantum computing enhanced imaging will be discussed.
Dr. Mikhail Lukin is the Joshua and Beth Friedman University Professor of Physics at Harvard University, where he also serves as Co-Director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative. Dr. Lukin received his Ph.D. in physics from Texas A&M University. Dr. Lukin’s research focuses on quantum optics and quantum information science, with an emphasis on controlling strongly interacting atomic, optical, and solid-state systems. His work explores the quantum dynamics of many-body systems and develops novel applications in quantum computing, quantum simulation, quantum communication, and metrology. Dr. Lukin has pioneered advances in neutral atom quantum computing, quantum networking, and quantum sensing with both atomic and atom-like solid-state systems. Dr. Lukin has authored more than 540 scientific publications and is a member or fellow of the National Academy of Sciences, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Physical Society, and Optica. His honors include the Physics World Breakthrough of the Year (2024), Falling Walls Breakthrough of the Year in Physical Sciences (2023), the International Quantum Award (2022), the Norman F. Ramsey Prize of the American Physical Society (2022), the Charles Hard Townes Award of Optica (2021), the George Gamow Award (2020), and the Vannevar Bush Faculty Fellowship (2015). Earlier in his career, Dr. Lukin was recognized with the Alfred P. Sloan Fellowship, the Packard Fellowship for Science and Engineering, and the NSF CAREER Award. Today, Dr. Lukin continues to advance quantum information science through both research and leadership, helping shape the future of computing, communication, and measurement at the frontiers of physics.

events.title: ESE Seminar - Ruben Juanes: "Photoporomechanics: Towards stress-tensor tomography in 3D granular media"
events.abstract:
Abstract
Ruben Juanes (joint work with Wei Li, Yue Meng, Shiyao Wang)
Photoporomechanics: Towards stress-tensor tomography in 3D granular mediaRuben Juanes (joint work with Wei Li, Yue Meng, Shiyao Wang)At a fundamental level, the macroscopic response of granular media depends on the spatial organization of contact forces between grains—the so-called force chains. Despite their critical importance, force chains in granular media have been characterized and analyzed almost exclusively in 2D systems. To address this knowledge gap, we recently developed a new approach: a tomographic imaging technique (interference optical projection tomography, or IOPT), which by combining the principles of photoelasticity and tomography, provides direct visualization of the particles’ force network, thus circumventing the need of constitutive models of particle-particle contact (Li and Juanes, 2024). With our novel experimental technique, we provide the microscopic explanation for why a pack of angular particles is stronger than one of round particles: they form interconnected force networks that are less likely to buckle when under stress than the isolated chains in a pack of round particles.While early results show the potential of our approach, currently this new technique is limited to reconstructing the 3D scalar field of stress-anisotropy under axisymmetric stressconditions, for example, triaxial shear. Here, we present the reconstruction of the grain-scale full tensor field in 3D (stress-tensor tomography) and focus on the study of the 3D internal stresses in a single particle subject to arbitrary loading conditions. If time permits, we will present early results extending the experimentation, modeling, and inversion of the stress field from the single-particle scale to the ensemble-scale of 3D granular packs. The ability to interrogate the grain-scale stresses in granular media will enable new understanding of granular media and help predict the behavior of fluid-coupled granular media in landslides, liquefaction, and earthquakes.
Bio
Ruben Juanes is professor in Civil and Environmental Engineering, and Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences at MIT, where he has been since 2006. He is an expert in fluid flow through porous media and in geomechanics, and has applied his research to the fields of energy resources, carbon capture and storage, gas hydrates, water infiltration and soil irrigation, and induced seismicity. He holds an undergraduate degree from University of A Coruña (Spain) and graduate degrees from UC Berkeley, all in Civil and Environmental Engineering. He is a fellow of the American Geophysical Union and the American Physical Society.
References
Li, W., & Juanes, R. (2024). Dynamic imaging of force chains in 3D granular media. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 121(14), e2319160121.

events.title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Gregor Steinbrügge- "Coupled Thermal-Orbital Evolution of the Galilean Satellites"
events.abstract:
Io's volcanism and Europa's surface bear witness to the dynamics driven by tidal interactions of the Galilean moons with Jupiter. While Europa and Ganymede host subsurface oceans, which makes them prime candidates for habitability, tidal heating is unlikely to have been constant over the age of the Laplace resonance. In this talk I will revisit the coupled thermal–orbital evolution of the Galilean satellites using the astrometric and geophysical constraints obtained over the past years. The Juno mission has provided additional data about geodetic parameters and recent ground-based observations indicate that Io has been volcanically active for most of its history, with potentially higher activity at earlier times. We also apply lessons learned from the Saturn system, particularly informed by the Cassini mission, to investigate the possibility of ‘resonance locking’ as the dominant mechanism driving the orbital migration of Io. Our analysis shows that considering ‘resonance locking’ in the Jovian system could reveal new evolutionary paths with early tidal dissipation in Ganymede and periodic inward migration of Io. I will further discuss the implications for the structure and dynamics of Europa’s ice shell if ‘resonance’ locking is at play. Finally, I will outline how some of these hypotheses can be tested by the Europa Clipper mission.
Gregor Steinbrügge received his M.S. degree in physics from the Free University of Berlin, Germany, in 2013 and completed his Ph.D. at the Institute of Geodesy and Geoinformation Science of the Technical University of Berlin, Germany, in 2018. His thesis on tidal interactions across the Solar System was completed in collaboration with the Institute of Planetary Research at the German Aerospace Center (DLR). He is a Research Scientist at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and the Investigation Scientist for REASON (Radar for Europa Assessment and Sounding: Ocean to Near-surface). He is also a Co-Investigator on the BepiColombo Laser Altimeter (BELA) and on the Ganymede Laser Altimeter (GALA) aboard Juice, and a member of the VenSAR science team on ESA's EnVision mission. His research focuses on tidal interactions of planetary bodies in our Solar System, ice geophysics, radar and laser geodesy, and the development of innovative mission instrumentation.
Speaker suggested reading: Hussmann, H., & Spohn, T. (2004). Thermal-orbital evolution of Io and Europa. Icarus, 171(2), 391–410. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2004.05.020

STANFORD CENTER FOR PRECISION MENTAL HEALTH SEMINAR SERIES

FEAUTURED PRESENTATION
Talk Title: Heart-brain interactions driving cardiovascular dysfunction
Speaker: Alexander R. Nectow, MD, PhD Assistant Professor, Department of Medicine, Columbia University
DATE & TIME: Tuesday, Dec 1, 2026 | 9:30 - 10:30 AM PST
LOCATION: Lokey Stem Cell Research Building , G1161 Large Conference Room
REGISTER HERE
ABOUT THE TALK
Stress is a major trigger of arrhythmia, yet the mechanisms underlying these effects remain poorly defined. Using a genetic model of ventricular tachycardia (VT), we find that naturalistic emotional stressors rapidly provoke malignant arrhythmias in vulnerable hearts. By tracing back from sympathetic neurons innervating myocardium, we identify a multi-synaptic, brain-to-heart circuit originating within the midbrain, which is required for stress-induced VT. Strikingly, activation of this pathway induces VT within seconds, suggesting that central neuronal control of the heart is an important arrhythmogenic trigger. Together, this work identifies a brain-to-heart circuit responsible for triggering stress-induced arrhythmias and points toward circuit-directed therapies for this class of tachyarrhythmias.
ABOUT THE SPEAKER
Alexander Nectow, MD, PhD, is an Assistant Professor at Columbia University who has established the dorsal raphe nucleus as a new center in the brain's control of feeding and energy homeostasis. The group has identified defined dorsal raphe and adjacent brainstem cell populations whose activity drives food intake and energy expenditure using cell type-specific molecular profiling and circuit dissection tools, many developed in the lab. Together, this work has established new principles for the neural control of feeding at the cell type and circuit level. The lab now runs two active programs: continued mechanistic work on the neural control of energy balance, and a newer effort on the brain-heart axis – the central afferent and efferent circuits that govern cardiac physiology, and their contributions to arrhythmia and other cardiovascular disease

events.title: PhD Dissertation Defense: Tianyu Lu
events.abstract:
Title: Generative Models for Protein Design
Abstract: Generative models are flexible tools with which we can model complex data distributions. When applied to proteins, we aim to build a model capable of generalizing the patterns observed in natural protein sequence/structure/function to the design of novel proteins conditioned on arbitrary desired functions. Samples from a generative model are hypotheses of the physical world. I show that generative models can expand functional space beyond what nature has already explored. First, I propose the SHAPES framework to benchmark how well generative models cover the distribution of native protein structures. I present the perspective of an oracle trap, in which filtering designs by structure prediction models leads to oversampling of idealized helices and undersampling of loops. Second, I present Protpardelle-1c, a collection of generative models of protein structure with improved conditional generation capabilities. I focus on motif scaffolding, in which we can condition on function by identifying a substructure/subsequence pair which geometrically defines the desired function. Protpardelle-1c excels on MotifBench, a standardized benchmark for motif scaffolding, proposing designable scaffolds to problems previously unsolved by other models. Finally, I apply generative models to the design of lanthanide binding proteins. I demonstrate how partial diffusion with Protpardelle-1c allows access to local perturbations of the lanmodulin fold to unearth a previously unexplored sequence space which has inverted rare earth selectivity, favoring heavy rare earths over light rare earths. Given a feedstock initially enriched in La/Ce (70%), the designed protein removes ~99% of lanthanum and cerium to enrich for more valuable heavy rare earths. I also validate motif scaffolding experimentally, showing that EF hands hosted in novel non-lanmodulin scaffolds recapitulate their intended selectivity profiles, and use this to probe the modularity of selectivity and the interplay between motif and scaffold.

In this webinar with a Stanford physician who specializes in diabetes, you will learn why blood glucose changes during and after movement and how to use exercise safely to help steady your numbers. events.title: Ergodic Theory, categorically
events.abstract: In recent years, categorical treatments of famous theorems about properties of invariant measures have emerged. Among them are the de Finetti Theorem, the strong law of large numbers and ergodic decompositions. Here, we synthesize these developments by introducing the concept of a mixing morphism for an abstract dynamical system in a Markov category. It axiomatizes the idea of finding an average of the dynamics that is itself invariant, which is closely tied to the Pointwise Ergodic Theorem. In this talk, we will explore the abstract consequences of having a mixing morphism as well as several concrete instantiations in familiar Markov categories - for general probabilistic systems, linear systems with Gaussian noise, and possibilistic uncertainty.

Bio: Konstantina “Tina” Stankovic, MD, PhD, FACS is the Bertarelli Foundation Professor and Chair of the Department of Otolaryngology – Head & Neck Surgery at Stanford University School of Medicine, and professor, by courtesy, of Neurosurgery. She is a Harvard-trained ear and skull-base surgeon and a Massachusetts Institute of Technology-trained auditory neuroscientist. Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been used in many areas of medicine, and large language models (LLMs) have shown potential utility for various clinical applications. However, to determine if LLMs can accelerate the pace of genetic diagnosis and discovery, we examined whether recently developed LLMs (Med-PaLM 2 and Gemini) could assist in solving four types of genetic problems, which had sequentially increased complexity. First, in response to free-text input, Med-PaLM 2 correctly identified murine genes with experimentally verified causative genetic factors for six previously studied murine models for biomedical traits. Second, Med-PaLM 2 identified a novel causative murine genetic factor for spontaneous hearing loss that was validated using knock-in mice. Third, we developed a retrieval and grounding pipeline that enabled Gemini 2.5 Pro to analyze large lists of genes with genetic variants, which were identified in the genomic sequences of 20 human subjects with hearing loss; and it identified causative genetic factors for 80% of these subjects. Fourth, we developed a genetic analysis pipeline, which enabled the modified Gemini 2.5 Pro without any task-specific fine-tuning to identify causative genetic factors for six subjects with rare genetic diseases that required 14 to 34 different terms to describe their multi-faceted symptom complex. These results demonstrate that an AI pipeline can facilitate genetic diagnosis and discovery in mice and humans.

Amy E. Herr
Chancellor’s Professor, Department of Bioengineering
University of California, Berkeley
Title: What Genes (and Transcripts) Can't Tell You: Single-Cell Proteomic Tools for Embryos to Ecosystems
Abstract: Proteins are the primary functional molecules of the cell. A protein’s molecular form, abundance, and subcellular localization control cellular decision-making in ways that DNA and RNA cannot predict. Even at single-cell resolution, sequencing tools are blind to proteoforms, post-translational modifications, and protein-level heterogeneity that distinguish one cell's functional state from another's. Inspired by how microfluidic innovations — from droplet encapsulation and flow cells to nanopore integration — enabled the single-cell sequencing revolution, my lab designs precision proteomic tools capable of capturing both cellular- and protein-level heterogeneity.
We pursue this vision across applications spanning clinical biomedicine to fundamental biology. In breast cancer, we partner with physician-scientists to assess whether patient-derived tumor organoids faithfully recapitulate the therapeutic responses of the patients from whom they were derived — deploying single-cell mass spectrometry proteomics to profile protein states across organoid cell populations with single-cell resolution. In developmental biology, we measure the proteomic basis of lineage commitment in individual blastomeres of pre-implantation mouse embryos, using same-cell assays that recover both protein and RNA from the same originating cell — eliminating the between-cell noise that confounds separate-cell multi-omic comparisons. We extend this ‘joint analyses’ approach to organoid-derived cells, by coupling proteome and open chromatin (snATAC-seq). At a global scale, we collaborate with marine biologists to identify the molecular drivers of coral bleaching, the breakdown of symbiosis between coral host cells and their algal partners that threatens reef ecosystems worldwide.
What unifies our questions is a shared analytical challenge: rare, precious, or highly heterogeneous cell populations where bulk averaging is not just imprecise but misleading. In many cases, there is a need for sub-cellular measurement insight. Across all of the applications, I will detail how microfluidic design seamlessly integrates unit functions, precisely controls transport and reaction, and scales up efficiently. I will also consider the opportunities these tools create as AI/ML models of cellular behavior (i.e., virtual cell initiatives) increasingly demand paired, ground-truth molecular measurements at single-cell resolution.
Bio: Amy E. Herr received a BS degree in Engineering & Applied Science from the California Institute of Technology and MS and PhD degrees in Mechanical Engineering from Stanford University, where she was an NSF Graduate Research Fellow. She holds a Chancellor’s Professorship at the University of California, Berkeley in the Department of Bioengineering and is a Chan Zuckerberg Biohub Investigator. Prior to joining UC Berkeley, she was a staff member in the Biosystems Research Group at Sandia National Laboratories (Livermore, CA). Her research interests include bioinstrumentation innovation to advance quantitation in the biosciences & biomedicine, in particular the study and application of electrokinetic phenomena in single-cell and sub-cellular analyses. Her pedagogical interests are in bioengineering design and transport. Professor Herr is an elected Fellow of the American Institute of Medical and Biological Engineering (AIMBE) and an elected member of the National Academy of Inventors (2017). She serves on the DARPA Biological Science and Technology (BSAT) working group and the Engineering Review Committee for Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. She is an Associate Editor at the Royal Society of Chemistry’s journal Lab on a Chip.

About the Seminar
"Traversing chemical space with reactive molecular dynamics - methods and applications"
Computational approaches have long been employed alongside experiment to understand the complex potential energy landscape and reaction pathways that connect reactants and products through intermediates and transition states. In this talk, I will present how computer simulations, powered by quantum chemistry, can augment chemical understanding by suggesting novel reaction pathways in addition to its usual role of supplying structures and numerical results. Our primary approach is the ab initio nanoreactor, a first-principles molecular dynamics simulation in which a time-dependent external potential induces high-energy molecular collisions leading to reactivity. I will present two example applications of the nanoreactor that provide chemical insights into challenging reactivity: the astrochemical synthesis of nitrogen-containing heterocycles, and the oligomerization of red phosphorus from diphosphorus. I will also present newly developed computational methods that promise to improve the efficiency and automation of characterizing reaction pathways, including a robust internal coordinate interpolation approach that yields high-quality initial guesses for reaction pathways.

Lee-Ping Wang studied Physics at UC Berkeley and completed his Ph.D. in Physical Chemistry at MIT in 2011. He had some of the most enjoyable years of his research career at Stanford where he did postdoctoral research in the groups of Todd Martinez and Vijay Pande. In 2015 Lee-Ping started a position of Assistant Professor in the Department of Chemistry at UC Davis, and he was promoted to Associate Professor in 2020. His main research focus is on developing computational methods and tools for molecular simulations, including tools for automated reaction discovery, and training molecular mechanics force fields.

events.abstract:
"Predicting Spectroscopic Responses and Reactivity in Condensed-Phase Environments: Mechanistic Insights into Photophysics and Catalysis"
Local molecular environments influence the structural dynamics and electronic properties of the systems and determine how molecules respond to light and undergo chemical reactions. Predicting these responses requires linking environmental effects to experimental observables and molecular functions. In this talk, I will present computational frameworks that connect environmental interactions with spectroscopic responses, photodynamic pathways, and catalytic behavior.
I will first introduce an ab initio approach to quantify the vibrational Stark effect and environment-induced frequency shifts. While experimental spectra provide an ensemble-averaged picture, simulations reveal how individual molecular conformations and their local electric fields contribute to their frequency shifts. I will then discuss the extension of this framework to liver alcohol dehydrogenase (LADH2), examining how the protein environment affects the vibrational frequencies of bonds involved in the reaction. These responses offer insights into the physical origins of catalytic rate enhancement and future mutation studies.
Next, I will present excited state dynamics studies of red fluorescent proteins. Excited-state simulations reveal how residue protonation states and hydrogen-bonding interactions regulate chromophore twisting and non-radiative decay. These mechanisms help predict differences in fluorescence brightness and suggest molecular features to target in future protein designs.
Together, these studies connect spectroscopic features to molecular-level mechanisms, providing a physical foundation for understanding and tuning molecular behavior in condensed-phase environments.

events.abstract:
"Automatically discovering multistep mechanisms for rapid reaction network construction"
Rapid and accurate construction of reaction networks (RN) is of paramount importance in chemistry. The rate limiting step in RN construction is finding relevant transition states (TS) on the potential energy surface. Algorithms like the Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) are standard workhorses when a reactant and product pair are known. However, these methods assume the input geometries are one TS away. This assumption is routinely broken when the input minima come from enhanced sampling dynamics or "template"-based approaches, where a multi-step mechanism is required to carry out the transformation, such as through rearrangements into reactive conformers. We present an adaptive algorithm that automatically identifies reaction intermediates and splits into separate path minimizations. Splitting enables competing pathway exploration, turning the TS search problem into a mini-network construction one. We showcase its potential and limitations using known multi-step reactions, successfully reproducing the mechanisms autonomously.

About the Seminar
"The cellular biophysics of biomolecular condensates and co-condensates"
Biomolecular condensate formation has emerged as a fundamental principle of subcellular organization, providing dynamic hubs that coordinate diverse biological activities. Despite rapid progress in the field, the biophysical rules driving condensate assembly and function remain incompletely understood, particularly as we now appreciate that many condensates involve more than a single driving molecular species. Here, using a combination of genetics, biochemistry, and advanced microscopy methods, we show that the interplay among multiple proteins and nucleic acids can lead to co-condensate formation, with properties and behaviors far more sophisticated than those arising from simple binary phase separation. By integrating inputs cooperatively or anti-cooperatively, co-condensates modulate signaling pathways and gene regulatory programs across physiological and pathological contexts, including those formed by oncogenic fusion proteins and transcription factors. These findings illuminate a new framework of cellular regulation in both healthy and disease states.

events.abstract:
"Competition between two ancestral RNA modifying enzymes sets tRNA T-loop modification chemistries and tunes translation in human cells"
Transfer RNAs that decode mRNA during protein synthesis are the most densely modified RNAs in the cell. Uridine at position 54 is among the most evolutionarily conserved modified positions of the tRNA T-loop. Bacteria methylate this position to m5U54 while archaea pseudouridylate it to Ψ54. Humans inherited and kept enzymes from both ancestral lineages. However, the consequences of this dual inheritance and the functions of these modifications are unexplored. To address this, we depleted TRMT2A, the enzyme that installs m5U54, and profiled tRNAs using Nanopore and quantitative pseudouridine-sensitive tRNA sequencing, and mass spectrometry. We discovered that TRMT2A and the pseudouridine synthase PUS10 compete to modify the same uridine and set tRNA-specific m5U54 and Ψ54 occupancies. The competition shapes the proteome in a codon-specific manner, codons decoded by m5U54-modified tRNAs are translated more efficiently than those decoded by Ψ54-modified tRNAs. Further, we find a T-loop modification circuit that is inverted relative to the one defined in yeast. Together, our findings establish competition for distinct modifications at a single position as an epitranscriptomic mechanism of gene regulation and reveal that RNA modifications and their crosstalk circuits are neither universal nor static across domains of life.

events.title: Thesis Defense: Shuri Francis, Gaffney Group
events.abstract:
"Resolving the Charge Distributions and Lifetimes of Excited States in [Metal(diimine)(dithiolate)] Complexes with Ultrafast X-ray and Optical Absorption Spectroscopies"
"This thesis unravels the interplay between covalent metal–ligand interactions and the excited state charge distributions and lifetimes of planar d8 [M(diimine)(dithiolate)] complexes (M = Pt, Ni) with bipyridyl (bpy) and benzene-1,2-dithiolate (bdt) ligands, going beyond what was previously possible with nanosecond resolution optical transient absorption and photoemission spectroscopies. Due to the disproportionately strong metal–dithiolate orbital mixing that characterizes [M(R2-bpy)(bdt)] systems, the tunable, visible light HOMO → LUMO absorption bands of these chromophores have metal-and-dithiolate ligand → diimine ligand charge transfer (MLL’CT) character. The Pt (5d) congeners have been studied for decades and developed primarily as photosensitizers because of their long-lived 3MLL’CT states. Substituting the metal center renders these complexes non-luminescent, convoluting efforts to design more earth-abundant and cost-effective Ni (3d) alternatives. Towards rationally designing structurally asymmetric, photo-active systems that utilize charge transfer and/or metal-centered (d-d) excited states for photochemistry, it is necessary to understand how manipulating molecular design parameters controls excited state dynamics and structure immediately after light absorption.
Combining theoretical electronic structure studies with femtosecond resolution X-ray (XTA) and optical (OTA) transient absorption spectroscopies bridges this gap by elucidating fundamental design strategies to optimize excited state charge distributions and lifetimes in photo-active, mixed-ligand donor–acceptor transition metal complexes. Pt 2p3/2 (L3-edge) and Ni 1s (K-edge) XTA spectroscopies directly probe the metal center-specific excited state relaxation mechanisms of [M(bpy)(bdt)] complexes, implicating the low-lying unoccupied Ni 3dyz orbital of [Ni(bpy)(bdt)] in deactivating the MLL’CT state that is long-lived in [Pt(bpy)(bdt)]. This deactivation fosters, as the dominant decay channel, the sub-picosecond formation of a meta-stable triplet ligand field (3LF, ‘d-d’ symmetry) excited state that distorts along a tetrahedral structural coordinate. Moving from inner-sphere to outer-sphere modifications, OTA spectroscopy demonstrates that diimine ligand functionalization and solvation effects can be used to systematically adjust the excited state lifetime of [Ni(R2-bpy)(bdt)] systems. By integrating time-independent and time-dependent density functional theory (DFT/TDDFT) with the aforementioned ultrafast transient absorption experiments, pseudo-tetrahedral structural reorganization in the 3LF state is revealed to induce dynamic changes in metal–ligand orbital mixing, thereby reversing the directionality of the ligand-to-ligand charge transfer. In contrast, the long-lived 3MLL’CT state of [Pt(bpy)(bdt)] undergoes planar structural relaxation and maintains strong metal–dithiolate covalency. Unlike traditional metal-centered excited states, DFT calculations also show that diimine substituent groups and solvent polarity can be used to independently strengthen or weaken the partial metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) character that strong metal–ligand covalency grants the pseudo-tetrahedral 3LF state of [Ni(R2-bpy)(bdt)] complexes."

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar: Professor AJ Boydston, University of Wisconsin–Madison
events.abstract:
About the Seminar
"Photocatalysis to Enable Metal-Free ROMP and Multimaterial 3DP of Electronic Devices"
Our group integrates fundamental and applied research within the scope of soft materials. In this seminar, we will discuss a new mechanism for ring-opening metathesis polymerization that is now a centerpiece of our program. The approach leverages visible light photoredox catalysis to allow for the use of organic initiators, in contrast to widely used metal-alkylidene initiators. Studies on our mechanistic hypothesis have yielded an exciting interplay of challenges and opportunities, often with one disguised as the other. We will share our findings that include methods for stereocontrol, chain transfer, and increasing functional group compatibility, as well as our adventures into the applied and commercial sectors. Additionally, we will present a breakthrough application of photocatalysis in the field of 3D printing. Our bottom-up approach to multimaterial 3D printing leverages wavelength selectivity and chemical orthogonality to enable direct 3D printing of functioning electronic circuits. The technology build from our platform of Multimaterial Actinic Spatial Control (MASC) 3D printing and allows for simultaneous synthesis of insulating dielectric materials and metallic conductors from single, homogeneous resin formulations.
About the Speaker
Dr. Boydston began studying chemistry as an undergraduate at the University of Oregon under the guidance of Professor Michael M. Haley. His research focused on the synthesis and study of dehydrobenzoannulenes. After completing BS and MS degrees, he began doctoral research at the University of Texas at Austin. In 2005, Dr. Boydston joined the group of Professor Christopher W. Bielawski and was co-advised by Professor C. Grant Willson. Dr. Boydston completed his thesis research focused on the synthesis and applications of annulated bis(imidazolium) chromophores in 2007. After graduating, he moved to Pasadena, California to take an NIH postdoctoral position at the California Institute of Technology. There, he worked under the mentorship of Professor Robert H. Grubbs to develop new catalysts and methods for the synthesis and characterization of functionalized cyclic polymers. He returned to the Pacific Northwest as an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of Washington in the summer of 2010 and was promoted to Associate Professor with tenure in 2016. In August 2018, he moved to the Department of Chemistry at the University of Wisconsin as an Associate Professor of Chemistry and Yamamoto Family Professor of Chemistry. His research group currently focuses on developments in the areas of electro-organic synthesis, photoredox catalysis, polymer synthesis, mechanochemical transduction, triggered depolymerizations, polymers for therapeutic applications, and additive manufacturing (3D printing). His research and teaching efforts have been recognized through the NSF CAREER Award, Army Research Office Young Investigator Award, Cottrell Scholar Award, Camille Dreyfus Teacher-Scholar Award, and University of Washington Distinguished Teaching Award.
Host: Yan Xia

events.title: Thesis Defense: Frank Hu, Markland Group
events.abstract:
"Development of language modeling for chemical analysis and design"
Generative modeling techniques offer the opportunity to achieve intelligent and efficient molecular analysis and design, making their development critically important in areas ranging from small-molecule lead optimization to materials discovery. Language modeling techniques in particular have proven effective at navigating highly combinatorial, discrete design spaces, suggesting that similar approaches could transform molecular design. In this dissertation, I develop language-model-based methods for molecular applications. Beginning with the problem of property-directed generative design, I present an energy-based alignment algorithm for chemical language models that yields highly scalable and sample-efficient molecular generators. Next, I apply chemical language models to spectroscopic analysis by designing, implementing, scaling, and post-training an end-to-end deep learning model for small-molecule structure elucidation from one-dimensional NMR spectra, achieving accurate and efficient elucidation for systems with as many as 40 non-hydrogen atoms. I then extend this framework with retrosynthetic context to enable context-aware structure elucidation, substantially improving accuracy without degrading performance when only spectra are available. Finally, I demonstrate how multifidelity asynchronous reinforcement learning with large language models (LLMs) can achieve frontier-level performance in small-molecule lead optimization against an expensive in silico oracle. Together, these projects explore how neural sequence models can inform both the understanding and the practice of chemistry.

events.title: Thesis Defense: Braxton Bell, Huang Group
events.abstract:
"Computational design of chemically modified cyclic peptide binders"
Cyclic peptides are an exciting therapeutic modality as they bridge the gap between small molecule drugs and biologics like antibodies. Currently, the primary strategy for identifying cyclic peptide binders is through high throughput experimental screening of combinatorial libraries, offering little control over physicochemical properties or binding epitope. Recent deep learning-based computational tools can design cyclic peptide binders, but they are largely limited to modeling amide- and disulfide-closed macrocycles. We developed a structure-based computational method that can be used to design cyclic peptide binders with arbitrary chemical modifications and cyclization chemistries. For designing novel interfaces, we first employed a tertiary motif search approach by mining the Protein Data Bank for proteins containing structural elements resembling the target’s epitope surface. We extracted shape-complementary fragments interacting with this surface and then designed molecules exploiting these binding modes using a mixture of molecular dynamics and generative modeling to realize the peptide backbones. In benchmarks, our approach was competitive with existing deep learning-based approaches for interface design by in silico metrics while still supporting exotic chemistries. Experimentally, we designed and characterized TBMB-crosslinked bicycles and thioether-closed macrocycles against three target proteins: MDM2, B7-H3, and TROP2. Coupling design with high-throughput screening of focused libraries using cDNA display, we identified and matured our lead peptides to low nanomolar affinity. This work provides a framework for the development of the next generation of cyclic peptide design methods.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar: Professor Brooks Abel, University of California, Berkeley
events.abstract:
About the Seminar
"Organocatalysts for Controlled Cationic Ring-Opening Polymerizations"
Extensive efforts have been made to synthesize polymers derived from heterocyclic monomers including lactones, lactams, and epoxides among other monomers, and numerous synthetic routes have been developed for their controlled syntheses using anionic ring-opening polymerization (AROP) and coordination catalyst systems. Less explored but equally promising as sustainable materials are polymers derived from heterocyclic monomers that are best polymerized by cationic ring-opening polymerization (CROP). Polymers synthesized by CROP comprise a diverse range of functional groups including acetals, orthoesters, ethers, phosphates, and disulfides among others. Additionally, polymers synthesized by CROP have been explored for their biodegradability and chemical recycling to monomer. However, despite more than half a century of development, CROP of heterocyclic monomers has not yet reached the same level of control over molecular weight, microstructure, architecture, and stereochemistry as has been achieved for AROP systems. This is largely due to undesirable Lewis acid-base interactions between the CROP catalyst and heterocyclic monomer. This presentation will provide an overview of our recent efforts toward the development of organocatalysts for cationic ring-opening polymerizations.
About the Speaker
Brooks Abel is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Chemistry at the University of California, Berkeley and staff scientist in the Materials Science Division at LBL. He received a B. S. in Polymer Science and a Ph.D. in Polymer Science and Engineering (NSF Graduate Fellowship) from the University of Southern Mississippi. His Ph.D. work under the advisement of Prof. Charles McCormick focused on synthesizing stimuli-responsive water-soluble polymers using controlled radical polymerizations for applications such as drug delivery and oil/water remediation. Following his graduate studies, he worked as a postdoctoral researcher with Prof. Geoffrey Coates at Cornell University (2017-2021) where he developed bifunctional Lewis acid catalysts for the alternating ring-opening copolymerization of epoxides and cyclic anhydrides to synthesize well-defined polyesters. While at Cornell, he also developed new methods for living cationic ring-opening polymerization of cyclic acetals, enabling the synthesis of ultra-high molecular weight polyacetal thermoplastics with capable of near-quantitative chemical recycling back to monomer. His independent research interests lie in the areas of sustainable polymer organic chemistry, main group polymerization catalysis, and ionic ring-opening polymerizations.
Host: Yan Xia

events.title: Thesis Defense: Ben Charnay, Kanan Group
events.abstract:
"Understanding and Engineering Ion Transport: Molecular Mechanisms and Electrochemical Devices for Sustainability"
Ion transport governs the efficiency of electrochemical technologies central to a sustainable future, from electrolyzers to batteries and their recycling. In this talk, I will discuss how ion transport can be engineered at the device level and understood at the molecular level. I will first present a membrane-free cell, designed with the aid of ion transport modeling, that produces acid and base from water using a porous separator in place of ion exchange membranes. By exploiting competitive rather than selective transport, it tolerates impurities and requires less energy than membrane-based systems. I will show its application to CO₂ removal from air and to lithium-ion battery recycling, where it regenerates concentrated acid from Li₂SO₄ waste.
I will then examine how ions influence one another's transport in concentrated aqueous electrolytes. Using ultramicroelectrode measurements in tandem with ultrafast optical Kerr effect spectroscopy, I will show that alkali cations suppress hydroxide diffusion by up to 36% (K⁺ < Na⁺ < Li⁺), by slowing Grotthuss proton hopping.

events.title: Recent progress in Bridgeland stability conditions
events.abstract: Bridgeland stability conditions provide a powerful tool for studying complexes of coherent sheaves on algebraic varieties. I will discuss some recent progress on their existence, moduli spaces of stable objects, Bogomolov-type inequalities, and related applications.

events.title: How to construct a quantum Markov chain
events.abstract: Classical Markov chains and Monte Carlo methods have driven major advances in statistical physics, probability, and modern computation. In this talk, I will present a general construction of quantum Markov chains that provides both a rigorous quantum algorithmic framework for sampling Gibbs states and a physically consistent dynamical model of thermalization in noncommutative many-body quantum systems. Together, these perspectives reveal new mathematical challenges whose resolution could unlock useful early applications of quantum computers.
