Yuan Gao: TBA
Geometric configurations in sparse subsets of the integer lattice
events.abstract:
We study the problem of how dense a subset of the integer lattice can be without containing a similar copy of a given simplex. We give an overview of a functional analytic approach, that combines techniques of analytic number theory, the geometry of numbers and purely analytic tools, leading to power-saving bounds. Time permitting, we plan to discuss some extensions, such as configurations consisting of a simplex together with its barycentre - a geometric analogue of Roth’s theorem on three term arithmetic progressions.
This is joint work with Andrew Lott and Nagendar Reddy Ponagandla.

events.title: Support recovery of diffusion models under the manifold hypothesis
events.abstract: We study diffusion models under the manifold hypothesis with possibly large score estimation and discretization errors, and show that while they may not exactly recover the data distribution, they will recover the support (or data manifold). In continuous time, we show that even if the relative score estimation error is fixed (and not necessarily vanishing), then the rate at which the process approaches the support is $O(\sqrt{(T-t)|\log(T-t)|})$ as~$t \to T$, where~$T$ is the final time. In discrete time, we use geometric time steps with a fixed (non-vanishing) ratio and show that with a fixed relative score estimation error, the process approaches the data manifold exponentially with the number of iterations. The proof relies on controlling a Gaussian measure of a neighborhood of the cut-locus of the data manifold, which, in turn, uses arguments from computational real algebraic geometry. This is a joint work with A. Alieva, G. Iyer and A. Novikov.

events.title: Quadratic cones as Einstein integrability loci
events.abstract: For every homogeneous quadratic scheme $Q\subseteq\mathbb A^N_{\mathbb Q}$ and every $n\ge3$, we construct a simply connected, smooth projective $n$-fold with a negative Kähler-Einstein metric, second Betti number two, and full holonomy $U(n)$, such that its space of essential infinitesimal Einstein deformations, together with its integrable directions, is stably complex-linearly equivalent to $(\mathbb C^N,Q(\mathbb C))$. Every infinitesimal Einstein deformation extends to second order, and extension to third order is equivalent to integrability. Affine cones over arbitrary projective varieties defined over $\mathbb Q$, in suitable embeddings, therefore admit such realizations.

events.title: Spectral graph methods in analytic number theory
events.abstract: The methods introduced in the breakthrough paper of Helfgott and Radziwill in 2021, and subsequently extended in my own work, have been instrumental in obtaining remarkable results in analytic number theory, including the recent resolution of the two-point Chowla conjecture. In this talk, I will give an introduction to these techniques.

events.title: Hikita conjecture for quiver gauge theories
events.abstract: Hikita conjecture predicts a ring isomorphism between the cohomology ring of a symplectic resolution $\tilde X$ of a symplectic variety $X$ and the coordinate ring of the scheme theoretic fixed points in the symplectic dual variety $X^\vee$. Open AI announced a proof of this conjecture on Oct. 6 when $X$ is a quiver variety and $X^\vee$ is the corresponding Coulomb branch. I will explain symplectic duality, the statement of Hikita conjecture, and a few key points of Open AI proof.

Oscillation of graph eigenfunctions and its applications
events.abstract: Oscillation theory, originally due to Sturm, seeks to connect the number of sign changes of an eigenfunction of a self-adjoint operator to the label k of the corresponding eigenvalue. Its applications run in both directions: knowing k, one may wish to estimate the zero set, or the topology of its complement, useful in clustering and partitioning problems. Conversely, knowing an eigenvector (and thus the number of its sign changes), one may want to determine if it ist he ground state, useful in the linear stability analysis of solutions to nonlinear equations.Within the setting of generalized graph Laplacians, Fiedler's theorem says that the k-th eigenvector of a tree (a graph without cycles) changes sign across exactly k-1 edges. We present a formula for the number of sign changes on a general graph, which attributes the excess sign changes to the cycles in the graph and their intersections.This result has many interesting connections. First, it allows one to derive a simple formula for the effective mass tensor of a particular class of crystals (periodic lattices), namely the maximal abelian covers of finite graphs. Second, it can be used to efficiently determine stability of a stationary solution on a coupled oscillator network, such as the non-uniform Kuramoto model for the synchronization of a network of electrical oscillators. Finally, the determinant of the matrix which determines the excess sign changes is closely related to the graph's Kirchhoff polynomial (which counts the weighted spanning trees), hinting at connections to both Feynman amplitudes and matroids. Based on a joint work with Jared Bronski (UI Urbana-Champaign) and Mark Goresky (IAS Princeton).

events.title: An irreducible projective plane in 4-space
events.abstract: Until recently it was unknown whether every knotted projective plane in S^4 decomposes as a connected sum of a "trivial" projective plane and a knotted 2-sphere (the Kinoshita Conjecture). I'll talk about some classic constructions of knotted surfaces and how they motivated us to find an irreducible projective plane. This is joint work with Mark Hughes, Seungwon Kim, and Gheehyun Nahm.

events.title: Sharp time asymptotics in the nonlocal multi-dimensional Fisher-KPP equation
events.abstract: The problem under study is the evolution of the level sets in a nonlinear integro-differential equation, which involves a convolution kernel that is even, but not isotropic in space.One can show that the level sets expand in an asymptotically linear fashion, the asymptotic speed depending on the direction through an expression known as the Freidlin-Gärtner formula. The goal of the talk is to explore the corrections beyond the linear term.

events.title: Distinguishing statistics and shuffling cards
events.abstract: Distinguishing statistics are a fundamental tool for obtaining lower bounds on Markov chain mixing times. In this talk, we will give a general overview of the technique. Then we will provide some examples of its application to card shuffling. More specifically, we will discuss Uyemura-Reyes' work on the random-to-random shuffle in his Stanford PhD thesis, as well as my recent work on the shelf-shuffle and random-to-top shuffle. No prior knowledge of Markov chain mixing or card shuffling is assumed.

events.title: Jack Xin: TBA
Detection thresholds for random geometric graphs
events.abstract:
Random geometric graphs hide geometric structure inside an otherwise random-looking network: each vertex has a latent position on a high-dimensional sphere, and edges are formed between vertices that are sufficiently close. When can this hidden geometry be detected from the graph alone? In this talk, I will discuss recent results establishing indistinguishability from Erdős–Rényi random graphs above the conjectured sharp dimension threshold, whenever the average degree grows polynomially with the number of vertices.
This talk is based on joint work with Cheng Mao (Georgia Tech), Nike Sun (MIT), Yihong Wu (Yale), and Jialing Xu (Duke).

events.title: Singularity Formation in 3D Euler and Nonuniqueness in Unforced 3D Navier–Stokes: Computer-Assisted Proofs
events.abstract: OpenAI's recently announced construction of a finite-time singularity for the Navier–Stokes equations relies crucially on $C^\infty$ external forcing. After brief remarks on this development, I will present two computer-assisted proofs for unforced incompressible flows. The first establishes finite-time, nearly self-similar blowup for the three-dimensional axisymmetric Euler equations with smooth, finite-energy initial data in a domain with boundary. It uses nonlinear stability around an approximate self-similar profile. The second establishes nonuniqueness of Leray–Hopf solutions to the unforced three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations from a common nonsmooth, finite-energy initial velocity. Key ingredients include the construction of an exact forward self-similar profile and rigorous verification of an unstable eigenmode of the associated linearized operator. Both analyses share a central strategy: decomposing the linearized operator into a coercive part, controlled through sharp functional-analytic estimates in weighted spaces, and a finite-rank perturbation, rigorously estimated with computer assistance. The talk will highlight the complementary roles of stability and instability and how numerical observations can be transformed into rigorous results. The Euler work is joint with Jiajie Chen, and the Navier–Stokes work is joint with Yixuan Wang and Changhe Yang.

events.title: Number Theory
The Theory of Probabilistically Checkable Proofs
events.abstract:
Speaker: Dor Minzer (MIT)
Abstract: I will discuss the theory of PCPs, from its inception in the early 1990's until the current state of affairs. Our discussion will be centered around the field of hardness of approximation, and in particular explain how the Unique-Games Conjecture arose and the human work that has been done towards proving it over the years. We will say a few words about OpenAI's recent resolution of the Unique-Games Conjecture.

events.title: Number Theory
Large deviations of Brownian intersections
events.abstract: In this talk, we consider the upper-tail large deviations of intersections of Brownian motions. Apart from intrinsic interest, these quantities are also closely related to the parabolic Anderson model via the Feynman-Kac formula. We prove that the occupation measures of Brownian motions conditioned to have large intersections converge weakly, up to spatial shifts, to the measure whose density is the square of an optimizer of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality. The key tools are a compactification of the weak topology and an exponentially good approximation of the Brownian occupation measure.

Algebraic Geometry Seminar
Vlasov equation in fixed FLRW spacetime II
Sturmian discrete and metric graphs - appearance and absence of gaps.
events.abstract: We study the spectra of Sturmian Schroedinger operators on graphs (either metric or discrete).A Sturmian sequence is an aperiodic sequence which is determined by an irrational frequency.These sequences are used to form aperiodic graph structures.We consider the integrated density of states (IDS) for Schroedinger operators on such graphs.The gap labelling theory predicts all the possible gaps in the spectra of these operators.We explicitly compute the gap labels; we show which gaps appear in the spectrum and which are absent, and why.The talk is based on joint works with Siegfried Beckus, Raphael Loewy and Gilad Sofer.

events.series: Student Learning Seminar on Mathematics and Computation
events.abstract: We give an introduction to the mathematical theory behind diffusion models. Based on the notes https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.01693.

events.title: Capacities on dynamically convex toric domains and embedding obstructions
events.abstract: In this talk, I will introduce a sequence of symplectic capacities defined using cylindrical contact homology (CCH), based on unpublished work of Michael Hutchings and cobordism maps constructed by Hutchings and Jo Nelson. I will explain how topological constraints on holomorphic cylinders rule out certain terms in the CCH differential, while known capacity computations and cobordism maps force other terms to be nonzero. These arguments lead to explicit formulas for the differential and the capacities of four-dimensional monotone toric domains. I will conclude with examples of new symplectic embedding obstructions between monotone toric domains and discuss blind spots of CCH capacities.

events.title: Algebraic Geometry Seminar
Topology of Lagrangians via open-closed string topology
events.abstract: The topology of Lagrangian submanifolds in the standard symplectic vector space C^n is a fundamental, yet poorly understood, problem in symplectic topology. A related question, known as Maslov class rigidity, concerns constraints on the Maslov classes of Lagrangian embeddings in C^n. I will describe a new approach to these problems based on ideas from open-closed string topology. As applications, I will present new results on these questions, extending classical theorems of Viterbo, Cieliebak–Mohnke, Fukaya, and Irie.

events.title: The phase diagram of two-layer neural networks
events.abstract:
One of the most remarkable properties of modern AI systems is to learn and often memorize large training sets and yet generalize well to unseen data.
I will give an overview of work carried out over the past several years to undestand the interplay of overfitting and generalization in simple two layer networks.

events.title: Bounded gaps between primes via APs with partly smooth moduli
events.abstract: Building on Yitang Zhang's work on bounded gaps between primes, the Polymath project showed that there are infinitely many prime gaps which are no larger than 246. In this talk I will discuss how the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem can be combined with newer equidistribution estimates for primes in APs to obtain an improvement on Polymath's result. The key ingredient is a new choice of support for the functions appearing in the corresponding optimization problem for the GPY sieve. To choose this support, we produce various equidistribution conditions for moduli with a large smooth factor, and reduce the calculation of relevant integrals to matrix multiplication and recursion.

events.title: On filtration formula and nodal sets in min-max theory
events.abstract: There are many striking analogies between two areas of geometry: minimal surfaces theory (in particular min-max theory) and spectral geometry (in particular nodal geometry). These include asymptotic Weyl laws, multiplicity-one theorems, density results, and more. In this talk, I will discuss one approach to a rather philosophical question: What is the source of these similarities? Is there a deeper theory or principle that explains them? In particular, I will explain a counterexample to the asymptotic optimality conjecture of Marques and Neves, and how a less rigid notion of nodal sweepouts nevertheless recovers Gromov's volume spectrum. The talk is non-expert-friendly and assumes no background knowledge.

events.title: The Exact Overlaps Conjecture on the Dimension of Self-Similar Measures
events.abstract:
Stationary measures are central objects in dynamics and probability. Self-similar measures are among the simplest examples of stationary measures, yet they are intricate to study. A similarity is a map from R^d to itself that uniformly scales distances and a self-similar measure is a stationary measure arising from the action of contracting similarities on R^d. The support of a self-similar measure is called a self-similar set, which is a central object in fractal geometry. Examples for self-similar sets are the Sierpinski triangle or the Menger sponge. The central question of interest for self-similar sets is to determine their Hausdorff dimension. More generally, one can also study the dimension of self-similar measures.
The exact overlaps conjecture predicts a formula for the dimension of self-similar measures and therefore also of self-similar sets. I will present joint work with Samuel Kittle fully resolving the conjecture in dimension 1. Our proof was found with the help of GPT-6 Astra and published on the arXiv on the 7th of October, while the result was also contained in the announcement of OpenAI on the 6th of October as paper 148.

events.title: Bergman Distinguished Lecture: Large time behaviour in Fisher-KPP type equations
events.series: Stefan and Adele Bergman Memorial Lecture Series
events.abstract:
The question addressed in this talk is the precise time asymptotic location of the level sets of the solutions of a class of partial differential equations that are usually referred to as "of the Fisher-KPP type", the acronym standing for Kolmogorov, Petrovskii, Piskunov. These equations arise in biology, ecology or population genetics; but also in probability, in the theory of branching random walks.
The sharpest information has, for a long time, come from probabilistic analyses. The goal of the talk is to present an alternative point of view which opens the way to the understanding of new situations, such as, for instance, nonlocal models, or models in heterogeneous media.
You can learn more about Professor Jean-Michel Roquejoffre on his website.

events.abstract: I will give a general overview and explain how the models are used in practice and why we prefer diffusion models to their alternatives. Then, I will go a bit into reward tilting, if time permits.

events.title: Agentic AI for mathematical reasoning and verification
events.abstract: Well-designed agentic harnesses can substantially extend the capabilities of foundation models in mathematical reasoning and verification. I will illustrate this through case studies of three provers (Rethlas, Danus, and Pharos) and one verifier (OSVerify). I will also discuss the design philosophy behind these systems from a mathematician's perspective, and directions for future work.

events.title: Regularity Methods in Combinatorics, Number Theory, and Computer Science
events.abstract: Understanding the structure of large graphs is a fundamental problem, as it can yield critical insights into topics ranging from the spread of diseases to how the brain works to patterns in the primes. Szemerédi's regularity lemma gives a rough structural result for all graphs. It is one of the most powerful tools in graph theory, with many applications in combinatorics, number theory, and computer science. Roughly speaking, it says that every graph can be partitioned into a small number of parts such that between almost all pairs of parts the graph is random-like. Variants of the regularity lemma have since been established with many further applications. In this talk, I will introduce the regularity method and its applications, and survey recent progress in understanding the quantitative aspects of these results.

events.title: Higher-order paracontrolled calculus for geometric rough paths
events.abstract: We introduce the tools of higher-order paracontrolled calculus, developed originally in the works of Gubinelli-Imkeller-Perkowski and Bailleul-Bernicot, which provides a harmonic-analytic perspective on singular stochastic partial differential equations. We show how these methods can be adapted and extended to handle rough differential equations in a lower-regularity regime, and identify the necessary probabilistic data needed to give meaning to the equation. Part of our proof involves developing a general harmonic-analytic framework for proving commutator estimates which are necessary for expanding the solution to the equation, which is of independent interest.

Imagine a world where preparing food means implementing sophisticated recipes in an electric kitchen, and ingredients are approvisioned from a supermarket by car. In this world, when the car breaks down, or the supermarket is closed, or a power outage stops the appliances, or all recipes vanish, we'll believe we can't eat. I'd like to share with you a modest way in which I like to do mathematics.

events.title: Topology, Morse Index, and Area of Minimal Surfaces in Three-Manifolds
events.abstract: A foundational and fascinating theme in differential geometry is to understand how geometric quantities constrain topology. In this talk, we will explain how the topological complexity of minimal surfaces in closed three-manifolds can be controlled by their variational instability and area, and how positive Ricci or scalar curvature of the ambient manifold lead to stronger bounds depending only on the Morse index. Finally, we will discuss some consequences of these results for the topology of min–max minimal surfaces.

A quasipolynomial inverse theorem for the U^k(F_p^n) norm in the high characteristic
events.abstract: The inverse theory for Gowers uniformity norms is one of the central topics in additive combinatorics and one of the most important aspects of the theory is the question of bounds. In this talk, I will discuss a recent work, which proves a quasipolynomial inverse theorem for $mathsf{U}^k$ norm in $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ in the case of high characteristic (meaning $p \geq k$). I will discuss the key ingredients of the argument: the abstract Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers theorem, algebraic regularity method and the theory of multilinear maps defined on multilinear varieties. Along the way, I will highlight the differences from previous works in the inverse theory of uniformity norms.

Title: Quantum-Addressable Routing and Higgs Mode Spectroscopy with Superconducting Circuits
Abstract: This thesis explores two complementary approaches toward quantum computation using superconducting circuits by developing a gate-based quantum router for quantum information processing and probing the excitations of many-body modes using analog quantum simulation techniques. First, we implement a gate-efficient quantum-addressable router with four fixed-frequency transmons. This router can transfer quantum information to a superposition of two locations based on a quantum address. By combining a large ZZ-interaction with two-qubit transitions involving the third transmon eigenstate, we realize this routing protocol with only two native three-qubit gates. We develop techniques to carefully calibrate and benchmark its quantitative performance at 95.3%, establishing the router as a possible building block for applications such as quantum networks and quantum random access memories. Next, we engineer the Hamiltonian of a transmon lattice to directly implement the 2D unit-filling Bose-Hubbard model and perform spectroscopy on the Higgs mode. While the Higgs mode is challenging to detect on other platforms, we demonstrate precise, selective control over both the Higgs and Goldstone modes, which allows us to map their spectra across the Mott insulator to superfluid phase transition. We study how the interactions between these collective modes change qualitatively as a function of system size. Both projects use the multi-level physics of superconducting transmons as a resource, going beyond the two-level qubit approximation. Higher levels enable efficient swaps and influence the ZZ strength in the quantum router, while they set the on-site interaction strength and enable doublon readout in the Bose-Hubbard model. Together, these experiments demonstrate how careful control of superconducting circuits unlocks the ability to perform quantum information processing as well as analog quantum simulation of many-body physics."

Research Advisor: Noah Kurinsky
Public zoom link: https://stanford.zoom.us/j/92997243346
Title: Cryogenic Charge Sensing for Dark Matter Searches: Quantum Sensing and Narrow-Gap Materials
Abstract: Dark matter makes up about 85% of the matter in the universe, yet no direct-detection experiment has observed a confirmed (5σ) signal. With much of the GeV-scale parameter space now explored, sub-MeV dark matter remains largely unprobed because the eV-scale bandgaps of current semiconductor detectors set the lowest detectable dark matter mass. The SPLENDOR Collaboration’s approach to sub-MeV dark matter is to synthesize novel narrow-gap semiconductors with bandgaps of order 10–100 meV. Detecting ionization in these materials requires a new detector platform that allows candidate substrates to be swapped easily, without complex fabrication, while reaching sub-electron charge resolution. This talk presents SPLENDOR’s first charge amplifier, a two-stage design based on low-noise cryogenic transistors (CryoHEMTs), which achieved a charge resolution of about 20 electrons, with a projected resolution of about 3 electrons with amplifier improvements. This talk then presents a second charge amplifier based on superconducting quantum circuits, specifically a cavity-embedded Cooper pair transistor, including its design, initial performance, and projected charge sensitivity. This work pushed established CryoHEMT amplifiers toward their single-electron limit and produced an initial superconducting quantum circuit designed for charge sensing in macroscopic substrates.

events.abstract:
Ph.D. Candidate: Zachary Hulcher
Research Advisor: Hirohisa Tanaka
Public zoom link: https://stanford.zoom.us/j/99631033161
Title: Charged Kaon Reconstruction in Neutrino-Argon Interactions in the NuMI Off-Axis Neutrino Beam at ICARUS
Abstract: The liquid argon (LAr) time projection chamber (TPC), or LArTPC, is an advanced neutrino detection technology, developed to detect and image neutrino interactions while assisting measurements of their fundamental properties. One such LArTPC, the ICARUS (Imaging Cosmic And Rare Underground Signals) detector at Fermilab, offers 480 tons of liquid argon as a target for neutrinos from two beams of neutrinos, the BNB (Booster Neutrino Beam) and off-axis NuMI (Neutrinos at the Main Injector) beam. These beams enable a variety of physics measurements, from neutrino oscillation to higher energy neutrino interactions. This thesis demonstrates the reconstruction of an understudied neutrino interaction product, the neutrino-induced charged kaon K+, using the tools provided by the SPINE reconstruction framework. Future measurements of atmospheric ν-induced K+ production, leveraging the techniques herein, would constrain a major background for proton decay at a number of experiments. While most neutrino interaction topologies are best identified by the particles closest to the interaction itself, K+ are best identified by their decays, often at rest, to µ+νµ. Inspired by this, we develop a novel particle flow proxy connecting all such potential decays to original interaction products. This yields a selection of K+ decay at rest to µ+νµ with a nominal Monte Carlo (MC) efficiency of 53% and purity of 84%. By leveraging this complete particle propagation information, we select 22 ν-induced K+ → µ+νµ candidates compared with nominal MC predictions of 11.0 signal and 2.17 background events. This represents the heretofore largest sample of selected K+ candidates in LAr [1]. These efficiencies, purities, and yields depend on the nominal simulation, which simulates all K+ production through strangeness preserving interactions and does not include single K+ production. Systematic uncertainties are not propagated, and no cross-section measurement or discovery significance is claimed. Additionally, as we will show, these ν-induced K+ and the other uncommon particles produced in such interactions present multiple unique detector calibration targets. Herein we demonstrate both the range distribution for the nominally monoenergetic decay µ+ as well as a dE/dx proxy for kaons, both new potential in-situ calibration sources for LArTPCs.

events.title: Integrating statistics and AI for neuroscience research
events.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of the human brain, and their connections to neurological disorders, cognition, and normal development, is one of the most intriguing scientific questions. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and statistical methodology have created unprecedented opportunities, while many challenges remain. In this talk, I will provide an overview of several research directions pursued by our group integrating statistics and AI for neuroscience research. I will discuss how modern AI methods can facilitate statistical analysis of brain imaging data as well as how statistical principles can improve the development of AI models. I will illustrate with a number of case studies, highlighting the synergistic relationship between statistics and AI in advancing our understanding of the human brain.

events.title: Taming the statistical multiverse: Precise causal inference when reasonable analyses disagree
events.abstract:
When reasonable analyses of the same data conflict, it can be unclear what to conclude. We study one source of disagreement: which covariates to adjust for. Domain knowledge often leaves several adjustment sets plausible, and the resulting estimates can vary widely. Instead of asking how much conclusions vary for a fixed population, we ask: for which population do the covariate adjustments agree? We search for the closest such population, obtained by reweighting. For this population, we construct a single effect estimate and a confidence interval, valid if at least one candidate adjustment set satisfies ignorability. The interval's width shrinks at the usual 1/sqrt(n) rate, whereas disagreement among candidate analyses can persist even with arbitrarily large samples. In an application, our interval is about 77% narrower than the span of the candidate intervals. By changing the target population, we obtain precise inference even when it is unclear which covariates to adjust for.
This is based on joint work with Aditya Ghosh.

events.title: Generative AI and the Future of FPGA IP Development
events.abstract:
Abstract/Description:
The development of intellectual property (IP) for field-programmable gate arrays has traditionally relied on lengthy, manual cycles of specification, RTL design, verification, and timing closure. Generative AI is now altering each of these stages. This talk focuses on three areas in which the presenter has observed dramatic change in workflow: design space exploration, RTL generation, and timing signoff.
The presentation will outline the methodology adopted at Lattice Semiconductor and will review several success stories in which generative AI shortened development schedules and improved engineering productivity. Particular attention will be given to the practical aspects of the approach: where AI-assisted design delivers measurable value, where human architectural judgment remains essential, and how correctness and quality are assured in a hardware context where errors are costly.
Although the talk will not address testbench and verification creation or documentation in detail, similar implications apply in those domains, and many of the lessons presented will carry over to them. The broader implications for engineering education and research, including the skills future hardware engineers will require and the open problems that merit academic investigation, will be reserved for the question-and-answer session, where the speaker welcomes a candid, open discussion with the audience.
Speaker/Bio:
Rick Crotty is Senior Fellow and Chief FPGA Architect at Lattice Semiconductor, a position he has held since 2019. In this role, he guides the architectural direction of Lattice’s FPGA product portfolio.
From 2014 to 2019, he co-founded Andapt, Inc., an analog mixed-signal power management IC (PMIC) company. There he pioneered the use of FPGA-based control loops within PMIC silicon, bringing together programmable logic and power management.
Prior to Andapt, he spent 21 years at Xilinx, Inc., where he held a series of roles in FPGA applications, circuit design, and ultimately FPGA architecture. Across more than three decades in the industry, his career has spanned the full range of programmable logic, from circuit-level implementation to system-level architecture. He is a named inventor on 45 patents in FPGA and circuit design technologies.
He holds a B.S. in Electrical Engineering from Carnegie Mellon University and an M.S. in Computer Engineering from Santa Clara University.
